title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
excerpt:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affect...
body_text:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.

Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally.

The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.

A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society,” said Martin, adding that European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were “all connected”.

She added: “But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures.”

The Nato alliance continued to monitor the situation and was working closely with allies, according to a senior Nato military official.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries were continuing.

Several European media outlets in Bulgaria, Ireland, the UK and elsewhere reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats warned in an email of further actions against transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said. The Guardian has chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.

Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016. In a Telegram post on Friday the group’s founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement and said the group had not existed since 2021.

Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern.

“It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.

“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

Mark Rowley, the chief of London’s Metropolitan police, urged a measured response, saying past experience with the paramilitary Irish Republican Army offered valuable lessons.

He recalled the phrase “10p terrorism”, when a hoax bomb call made from a coin-operated phone box could disrupt an entire city, forcing authorities to distinguish between genuine and false threats.

The authorities would need to adapt to an evolving threat landscape involving actors around the world, some backed by hostile states, he said.

“We are going to have to adapt to that same methodology to make sure that we don’t overreact to every message we get online,” he told BBC Radio 4.

title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
excerpt:
Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children

A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all bu...
body_text:
Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children

A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.

The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".

Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.

Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Diana Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.

Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.

One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.

The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.

Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.

The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.

More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest

The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.

"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen", says Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje says a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.

"It was his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."

The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.

Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.

The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

title: Commuters and shoppers face disruption from tube driver strikes in run-up to Christmas
excerpt:
RMT union calls eight 24-hour strikes on London Underground in opposition to plans for four-day week

Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – inclu...
body_text:
RMT union calls eight 24-hour strikes on London Underground in opposition to plans for four-day week

Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – including six in the lead-up to Christmas – that threaten to bring transport chaos to the capital.

The drivers will start another series of 24-hour strikes in late November in opposition to plans for a four-day week – a proposal that has been warmly welcomed by the majority of London Underground drivers represented by the Aslef union.

Disruption could mean few tube trains over the last shopping weekend before Christmas, with strikes running from noon on Thursday 17 December and again on Saturday 19 December.

The 24-hour strikes will begin at noon on 26 November, followed by the Christmas industrial action, with two more strikes planned in early January and more in February.

The RMT claims the new four-day week, which Transport for London (TfL) has said would be voluntary, would “undermine existing agreements and worsen working conditions”.

Previous strikes earlier this year resulted in widespread disruption to London Underground services, although trains ran on most lines.

The RMT said it has yet to receive guarantees about drivers’ right to remain on existing five-day working arrangements. It believes the proposals would worsen shift times and certainty.

The RMT’s general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said: “London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers’ working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.

“Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years.

“This is not about improving work-life balance. It is about squeezing more work out of fewer drivers while giving management greater flexibility at the expense of our members.”

Similar, highly disruptive strikes took place in London in April and June, despite TfL insisting the proposals were completely voluntary, and the plans having been fully endorsed by the main drivers union, Aslef.

title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
excerpt: Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite imag...
body_text:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

At Karaj and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.

The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.

Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.

The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".

The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".

A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.

But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas.

A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.

Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."

What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?

title: European skies on high alert as more airlines receive bomb threats – Europe live
excerpt:
Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week leaving at least 35 planes searched or diverted before Friday

A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP alerts were also received fo...
body_text:
Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week leaving at least 35 planes searched or diverted before Friday

A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP alerts were also received for two flights to Sofia on Friday, and that both flights coming in from London Stansted Airport in Britain and from Brussels landed safely.

Looking at the airport’s arrivals board, that’d be W64328 from Brussels and FR1730 from London Stansted.

Multiple flights across Europe have been diverted or forced to make emergency landings following a series of bomb threats this week, prompting security checks and widespread disruption.

Are you on one of the affected flights or has your journey disrupted? What happened, and how did you feel? What information were you given by the airline or authorities, and how was the situation handled?

Meanwhile, Copenhagen police confirmed that it’s done with their checks at the Danish capital’s airport (10:48).

“We have been present solely as a security measure. It is therefore our assessment that there is no or has been any danger to passengers or others using the airport. We are investigating the new threats in line with the threats that arrived yesterday, and therefore have no further information.”

FlightRadar24 tracking service shows that some of these searches are making other planes circle near Prague Airport, with at least four planes currently holding near the airport.

We are also getting a bit more detail from the Prague airport authorities on disruptions that once again affected its operations this morning.

At least eight flights to and from Prague were hit by bomb threats, its spokesperson confirmed to AFP.

It concerned incoming flights from Denmark, Spain, and the UK, and outgoing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy, and the UK, Denisa Hejtmánková said.

A Romanian airline Tarom flight from Prague to Bucharest is the latest believed to be affected by today’s bomb threats.

The aircraft, operating flight number ROT226M, sent a squawk code of 7700 – general emergency – before landing safely in Bucharest. The threat was later confirmed to be unproven.

Romanian media, quoting airport and intelligence officials, reported that the incident was linked to the recent wave of bomb threats against civilian aviation in Europe.

We are now getting a line from the French PM’s office that four new bomb threats against aircraft flying over the French territory were received today.

All of ‌the planes landed safely and bomb dispersal units ‌are conducting inspections, with a ​probe underway to determine ⁠the origin of the ​threats affecting ​all ​of ​Europe, ‌the office ​said.

I will bring you more on this when we have it.

The Lisbon report turned out to be a hoax, the Portuguese police confirmed to AFP.

The Portuguese public broadcaster RTP reported more detail from the police statement, saying the threat concerned both the inbound FR8196 flight and the reverse leg from Lisbon to Rome, FR8197.

The authorities will now try to determine “the origin and circumstances of the threat,” RTP reported.

A Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon, flight number FR8196, was also targeted by a bomb threat, according to Portuguese media.

“The authorities are taking steps to assess and confirm the credibility of the threat,” CNN Portugal reported.

Italian news agency Ansa reported that the security alert was received by police via “a phone call from a law enforcement officer.”

A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome has been diverted to Venice following a bomb threat, Italy’s Ansa news agency reported.

The flight number W46136 turned around near Ferrara and performed a U-turn to land safely in Venice.

Bomb threats against Irish media organisations have disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches on Friday morning.

RTÉ Radio One’s Today With David McCullagh went off air on Friday morning and was replaced with music as staff huddled outside buildings at the national broadcaster’s Donnybrook campus.

Staff at other outlets including Newstalk Radio, Today FM, Virgin Media and the Irish Independent were also evacuated.

Radio One’s regular broadcast returned to air at 10.13am. “It has been quite an interesting morning on RTÉ,” said McCullagh.

The email, received before 9am, said an explosion would detonate within 45 minutes, said McCullagh. Police with sniffer dogs remained at the campus.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told the programme that such threats had to be taken seriously and that Ireland’s police and defence forces would seek to identify those responsible. “It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society.”

The emailed threats came after separate threats to airlines on Thursday disrupted dozens of flights across Europe.

Prague police say they are also investigating threats against “a number of aircraft arriving at and departing from Prague airport.”

“In cooperation with Prague Airport, we have taken the necessary security measures with minimal impact on the airport’s normal operations. We continue to investigate the case,” they added.

They provided no details on what, if any, flights were affected.

Copenhagen police has just said that it is once again present at the city’s airport this morning following “threats directed at air traffic,” but insisted there was no danger to passengers.

“We are again present today at Copenhagen Airport in connection with threats directed at air traffic.

Our immediate assessment is that there is no or has been any danger to passengers or others using the airport. We are now investigating the incident and are visibly present at the airport. We currently have no further information.”

Yesterday, two unidentified planes were searched at Copenhagen airport as part of broader disruption across Europe.

In other news, EU leaders will discuss next week the vexed question of who speaks for Europe in talks on ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, following an angry rebuke from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls.

Italy is not a member of the E3, the trio of the UK, France and Germany, whose representatives met officials from Ukraine, the US and international bodies in Brussels earlier this week. Nor was it involved in other initiatives, such as a phone call between Vladimir Putin and the leaders of Norway and Finland, Jonas Gahr Støre and Alexander Stubb.

Meloni also highlighted an “informal” meeting between US, Ukrainian representatives, E3 national security advisers and European officials last month in Miami, which she said was only confirmed after the event by US sources.

Italy, however, Meloni noted, is invited to a meeting of the so-called Berlin format – a larger group of countries, which is due to meet on the sidelines of the European Political Community summit in Dublin next week.

Meloni insisted she was not seeking a place for Italy “in this or that format”, but complained about the proliferation of groups and lack of coordination. She is concerned that “in the absence of a mandate, commitments are negotiated which also our Nation will then be called upon to undertake.

“The outcome is far more important to us than the format itself. And to be able to aspire to shape such outcome, Europe needs to speak with a single, authoritative voice.”

In an emollient response to Meloni, European Council President António Costa promised to add the issue to the agenda of a one-day EU summit in Dublin next Friday, one day after the EPC.

“I also share your view that the European Union must be properly involved in discussions that shape Europe’s security and Ukraine’s future. The European Union’s participation must be organised in a manner that enables it to convey a clear and unified message, to defend its interests and to support Ukraine.”

But there is another view. Some European diplomats think the proliferation of formats and uncoordinated meetings is a sign that no real peace talks are taking place.

Airlines and airports across Europe are on high alert after a wave of hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week, leaving at least 35 planes searched or diverted.

Authorities will be hoping to see a quieter day today after yesterday’s disruptions.

But one of the incidents yesterday remains under closer scrutiny.

An Aer Lingus pilot who was flying from Dublin to Rome when the plane was diverted to the Évreux military base after a bomb threat is facing scrutiny from the French authorities after reportedly insisting on landing at a civilian airport.

Évreux’s public prosecutor, Rémi Coutin, told ICI Normandie that the pilot’s apparent initial refusal to land where instructed prompted the French military to scramble two fighter jets to intercept the aircraft.

The pilot and his co-pilot will be questioned to “understand what happened,” Coutin said, stressing that he could bring charges for refusing to cooperate with authorities.

In a statement to the Guardian, Aer Lingus backed the pilot, however, saying he and the crew acted “impeccably and thoroughly professional throughout” the incident.

“Safety and the care of our passengers is Aer Lingus’ top priority and this was upheld professionally by the captain and crew of the aircraft throughout in what were very challenging circumstances,” the airline said.

Elsewhere, we are expecting an update on the Belgian government as prime minister Bart De Wever meets King Philippe to discuss next steps after the collapse of budget negotiations.

Pope Leo is also off to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in his first overseas trip since his lung surgery last month.

It’s Friday, 6 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats exceed 250 House seats as blue wave sweeping Congress grows
excerpt:
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats, including in Ohio, Arizona and North Carolina; Ted Cruz calls election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’

Live results | Q&A: Ask your questi...
body_text:
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats, including in Ohio, Arizona and North Carolina; Ted Cruz calls election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’

Live results | Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win

The post-midterms market rout has been particularly painful for Elon Musk.

Musk (who put $446m of support into Republican campaigns), has lost around $113bn of wealth in the last two days.

This is because his two largest companies have both been badly hit in the sell-off.

Tesla fell 3.34% on Wednesday, as investors reacted to the Democrats’ electoral success, then 10.7% on Thursday. Musk owns 17.7% of the carmaker.

SpaceX lost 3.8% on Wednesday, then 9% yesterday – which also hurt Musk as he owns 10.3% of it.

In total, Musk’s paper wealth fell by $33.5bn on Wednesday, and then by another $79.7bn yesterday, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

Despite this, Musk is still the world’s richest person with a paper wealth of $785bn, more than double Jeff Bezos in second place with $370bn.

For the latest economic and financial news, you can follow our live blog here:

Tuesday night’s explosive rout of the Republican party was supercharged by the fury of Hispanic Americans who turned out in record numbers in key battlegrounds to protest the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant assault on their communities.

“Trump went against us,” said Benny Melendez from Weslaco, Texas. “He made us the target of ICE operations, so we decided to punish him by voting against his party. That’s what happened.”

Melendez, the owner of a small housebuilding company in south Texas, voted for Donald Trump in the presidential election two years ago, attracted by his promise to secure the Mexican border and improve the economy. But on Tuesday, he cast his vote for the Democrats in a display of pure anger.

Two of his cousins and up to 15 of his building workers have been picked up and deported to Mexico by ICE. When Melendez voted for Trump in 2024 he expected the immigration raids would focus on those with criminal records, he said, not his relatives and employees.

“They’re taking our neighbors. They’re taking our friends. They’re they’re taking our workers, and they’re taking our family members. This is an attack against our community.”

Melendez’s rage, replicated in the millions across Texas, Florida and other critical swing states, itself tells a story. It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.

Following a difficult set of midterm results for the Republican party, Donald Trump has spent much of this week talking up his renovation projects in Washington. Thursday brought the first official action of his post-midterms presidency – a proclamation designating the gold-adorned Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument.

With the dust still settling on the midterms, attention is already turning to the Republicans who might seek to lead the party into the next presidential race in 2028. JD Vance, Ted Cruz and Ron DeSantis are among those in the mix, as the Republican party begins to reckon with the fallout from its midterms performance.

In this report, my colleague Ariana Baio looks at the early jockeying, the potential contenders and what the midterm results could mean for the party’s future:

Welcome to our live coverage of the US midterm elections – here are some of the latest key developments.

A number of closely watched contests in the midterms are still to be called, including the final two US Senate races – in Mississippi and Alaska. The Democratic candidates are hoping to oust Republican incumbents to bolster their new majority in Congress. Right now, Democrats have a 106-seat majority as we await final results.

Democrats flipped another eight House seats, strengthening their majority in the lower chamber. Democrats are now leading Republicans 253 to 157, with 25 races left to call, as a number of GOP representatives felt the weight of the blue wave that has swept their party out of power. Republicans held on to two House seats in the west as congressman Mike Kennedy won re-election in Utah and Amanda McKinney won in Washington.

Democratic socialist Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles, eking out a narrow win over incumbent Karen Bass, in a major shake-up in local politics that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city. The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020.

Harmeet Dhillon, a key Trump ally, resigned from her position leading the justice department’s Civil Rights division. Attorney general Todd Blanche said he accepted her notice. Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections. Democrats are expected to use their power in taking control of Congress to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect in Michigan, said the new majority in the upper chamber needed “action” from their leader. On the campaign trail El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. Speaking to CNN, El-Sayed reiterated that Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, would be an “amazing Senate majority leader”, but didn’t completely rule out supporting Schumer.

Joining the chorus of Republicans who blasted their party’s midterms performance is Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who said the GOP were handed an “ass-kicking” in losing control of Congress. “It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” he said on his podcast.

The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm results.

Donald Trump signed a proclamation that preserves the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments in his first official action after the Republican wipeout.

title: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
excerpt:
Tundu Lissu says the trial is politically motivated

Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has ra...
body_text:
Tundu Lissu says the trial is politically motivated

Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.

But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.

Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.

The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.

"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.

"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.

He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.

He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.

Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.

Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.

Tundu Lissu - the great survivor of Tanzanian politics

Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws

WATCH: Tundu Lissu: A Fight Too Far? on BBC Africa Eye's YouTube channel

The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".

Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.

They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.

But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.

He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.

Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:

Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)

Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation

Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers

Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment

It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.

Widespread protests and a violent security crackdown after last year's elections left at least 500 people dead, authorities say

During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.

These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.

His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.

Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.

Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.

The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.

Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan won 98% of the vote in last year's election

Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.

He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.

In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.

He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.

The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years outside Tanzania.

He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.

Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.

His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.

But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.

Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.

His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.

Last week, rights group Amnesty International accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".

The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.

Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

title: UK government to extend controversial Palantir NHS contract as it draws up plan for British alternative – UK politics live
excerpt:
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls to axe US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, report says

Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extende...
body_text:
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls to axe US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, report says

Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported.

Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.

The system aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. But a review has concluded that removing Palantir from NHS data systems by triggering a break clause in its contract would be too disruptive, the FT reported.

Ministers instead plan to launch a procurement process for a UK tech alternative, with Palantir to potentially be replaced in two years.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.

The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.

The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”

double quotation markThe reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.

Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.

These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.

But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

double quotation markThe reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.

Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.

The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

double quotation markThe benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.

The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.

double quotation markOther settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.

Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party, who held Wednesday’s debate, said:

double quotation markWomen are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.

To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.

An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.

Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.

The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.

The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.

Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.

The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. The government has backed the use of smart meters and smart pre-pay meters to help households track their spending and avoid getting into arrears.

Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak.

The Home Secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.

Mark Nowak told ITV News: “I fully understand the need to carry a kirpan but surely that should be defined in law, in terms of size and type and whether it should be visible, and so on and so forth.

“And therefore, anything else should be made illegal.”

Asked about Mark Nowak’s suggestion, Mahmood told the same broadcaster:

double quotation markI haven’t taken any options off the table. I’m also not going in with a fixed mind about what the right clarifications of the law might be.

It’s important to get the right balance between religious expression in this country, which is something that many of us of a faith, including myself, hold very dearly, but do so in a way that is within what we expect of our citizens for the purposes of the criminal law.

Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch said lawmakers “do need to look at” knife laws.

Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.

Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives.

The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.

Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.

double quotation markWhether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it.

That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.

But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”

Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.

Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.

Burnham has spent much of his first few months in power announcing a series of “small fixes” to help improve people’s daily lives, while promising more radical change to come. The changes have included removing VAT from electricity bills, reducing bus fares and a £100 council tax rebate announced at the budget.

Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington, which said the agreement could instead be modelled on America’s Greenland deal with Denmark.

Shabana Mahmood’s changes to the migration system could harm women and children, a Labour MP has warned, as members of her own party continue to raise concerns with the home secretary’s proposals.

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
excerpt:
French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France

One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.

The ...
body_text:
French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France

One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.

The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.

The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".

The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.

The driver is reported to have been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.

Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.

Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.

"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."

Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".

Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."

Earlier, French education minister Édouard Geffray said the crash involved students.

He told reporters it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".

Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.

French Transport minister Philippe Tabarot, who was on his way to the area, said more than 100 firefighters had also been sent.

The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

title: Hoax or bomb threats? What we know about flight disruptions across Europe
excerpt:
Flights across Europe have been diverted, grounded and escorted by fighter jets in response to a wave of bomb threats, marking a second major outbreak of false alerts in less than a week.

On Thursday...
body_text:
Flights across Europe have been diverted, grounded and escorted by fighter jets in response to a wave of bomb threats, marking a second major outbreak of false alerts in less than a week.

On Thursday, planes departing from 16 countries, including Ireland, the United Kingdom, Spain and Denmark, were affected. Flights have either been forced to divert to alternate locations or undergo additional security checks. On Friday, the threats continued.

Authorities have deployed bomb disposal teams and military fighter jets in several countries. So far, security inspections following threats have yielded no evidence of explosives or suspicious materials on board aircraft, and no passenger has reported being harmed.

On Friday, a Ryanair flight landed in Lisbon, Portugal at 8am after a bomb threat was made by phone to the authorities, Italian media has reported. A security operation was mounted as soon as the plane landed. Separately, the control tower in Fiumicino, Italy, received an alert about a device aboard a Wizzair flight to Rome from Paris. The Wizzair flight was diverted to Venice where police were clearing the area around the plane.

On Thursday, there were numerous threats, including the following:

When an airline is notified of a threat to an aircraft, it is passed to a team of assessors, said Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation at BALPA, the British Airlines Pilots’ Association.

“These assessors use standard processes to grade the threat and decide whether the threat is red (credible), amber (partially credible) or green (not credible). Amber is not considered an appropriate assessment if the plane is airborne,” said Waites.

After receiving a threat, an aircraft is directed to an area well away from the airport buildings. Passengers are disembarked and screened while border police with sniffer dogs inspect the plane, according to an airport official.

The incidents follow a series of hoax bomb threats earlier this week. On Monday, a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that turned out to be without substance. On Tuesday, seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted because of malicious hoax bomb alerts.

And also this week, there have also been cyberattacks on supermarkets in several European cities, with hackers changing the temperature on refrigeration in an apparent attempt to spoil food.

Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said the scale and coordinated nature of these latest incidents are unusual.

“There are indeed individual airlines that experience a bomb threat every day, but most of those are very quickly evaluated and determined to be non-specific, and the aircraft do not divert,” said Baum.

What sets the latest incidents apart, he said, is that authorities across several European countries appear to be treating the threats as credible enough to require planes to land and undergo security inspections. Baum noted that each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000.

The UK’s government called the latest disruption “malicious hoax threats”. London Heathrow, the busiest airport for passenger traffic in Europe, was also targeted. It says it has one of the most robust aviation safety systems in the world, but countries still have to take the threats seriously and figure out how to stop any actors from creating further disruptions to air travel across Europe.

The European Commissioner for Transport said it is too early to say who’s behind these attacks or whether the incidents are even connected.

European governments have so far refrained from blaming anyone. But those which have supported Ukraine are wary of hybrid attacks. Germany has directly pointed the finger at Russia for recent drone incursions at Leipzig-Halle Airport. Moscow rejected the accusations.

EU officials are aware of the possibility that Russia would step up its hybrid campaign. In September, the Danish Defence Intelligence Service warned that this could happen to pressure adversaries in the West and NATO.

However, Moscow has denied being involved in the threats to aviation in Europe and there is no evidence of any involvement by Russia, Iran or any proxy groups linked to them.

title: ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters?
excerpt: From France and Italy to Spain and Albania, a regular feature of European protest movements has been the presence of a few hundred young people fully dressed in black, often engaged in physical violen...
body_text:
From France and Italy to Spain and Albania, a regular feature of European protest movements has been the presence of a few hundred young people fully dressed in black, often engaged in physical violence with law enforcement.

They have been seen smashing public and private property and setting fire to cars and buildings, and are accused of break-ins and stealing consumer goods – anything from food to jewellery.

Known as the “Black Bloc”, they have aggressive energy that can upend otherwise peaceful demonstrations by student groups and professional unions. While some say they bring attention to social, political, and economic inequalities, others condemn their violent methods, saying they distract from protesters’ legitimate demands.

“The movement started in the 1980s in Germany and came from a social movement called autonomia, or autonomy,” political science professor Francis Dupuis-Deri, at the University of Quebec in Montreal, told Al Jazeera. “They were against the state, capitalism, political parties, even communists and unions. They were more or less anarchists. They believe in living outside the system.”

Dupuis-Deri, who has authored a book on Black Blocs, explained that the anarchists’ idea was “simple”.

“You wear black suits, which was a punk fashion at the time, black leather jackets and cotton hoodies, motorcycle helmets, sunglasses and bandanas. This was a way of making sure they could not be recognised by the police … There is no leadership, no hierarchy, no superstars, no spokesperson, no press statements,” he said.

But he warned against associating the group with any political ideology, left or right, as there have been episodes of right-wing nationalist and neo-Nazi groups in Poland and Germany using Black Bloc attire and violent tactics, although not in recent years.

France has for weeks seen mass student and union demonstrations and is grappling with a high level of violence and property damage.

Al Jazeera contacted the office of a left-wing French member of the European Parliament (MEP), whose party has organised and supported recent nationwide rallies, about the black-clad protesters. But they said the issue was too sensitive to discuss.

“A few cases of violence are used by the government to criminalise our movement and our party, so we don’t want to enter the strategy of speaking about it,” said a person who was not authorised to speak officially on behalf of his elected official.

Italy has also witnessed violence in Rome, Milan, and Turin, with people clashing with police, setting bins and cars on fire, and in some cases causing extensive property damage and injuries.

“Frankly, I’m not aware of any movement inspired by the Black Blocs,” said Mario Furore, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the Five Star Movement. “In Milan, there have been incidents of looting and vandalism, and those responsible appear to have been very young, many of them minors.

“To me, this looks more like copycat behaviour and the influence of bad role models than the work of an organised network. However, it will be up to the judicial authorities investigating the incidents to establish the facts.”

The Black Bloc is not a homogeneous or organised movement with any known leadership or structure. It is also politically somewhat irrelevant because governments and law enforcement groups associate the groups with social protests, whether they are “copycats” or genuine.

Dupuis-Deri said the lack of organisational structure allows members to find each other quickly based on their attire, but they also congregate through word of mouth and form relationships over several demonstrations.

Mobility is a key feature of the movement.

While European governments have not publicised information on the recent demonstrations, Black Blocs are known for having crossed borders in the past to participate in demonstrations in other countries.

“They don’t have a membership roster, so no one really knows how many they are. Intelligence services number them around 5,000-7,000 in Europe, with a few hundred showing up in each demonstration,” said Dupuis-Deri.

Speaking in Parliament in January, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez referenced the group, saying: “Today, at every social demonstration of any significant size, we find Black Blocs who come to smash things and attack the internal security forces.”

A 2023 Italian government document on advanced training for police described the group, its aims, and tactics.

“With the aim of inciting vandalism and violence by infiltrating – and subsequently radicalising – demonstrations, the 1980s also saw the consolidation of a persistent anarcho-insurrectionist tactic: the use of small, loosely organised groups known as the ‘black bloc’,” the document said.

It added that they conduct reconnaissance of target locations well in advance of the planned unrest, dividing these areas into sectors assigned to specific teams, and execute diversionary tactics “carried out by one or more teams to draw the attention of law enforcement away from other groups, which are then free to carry out disruptive or destructive acts”.

The report said the Black Bloc has a “high degree of mobility” to maximise potential damage while minimising the risk of activists being arrested.

Before the recent demonstrations in Europe, perhaps the best-known Black Bloc performances were during the World Trade Organization ministerial meeting in Seattle, the United States, in 1999, and the June 2016 nationwide demonstrations in France against the Loi Travail or labour law.

In both cases, there were confrontations with police, with hundreds injured and arrested.

title: Macao court sentences pro-democracy ex-politician to 12.5 years in jail
excerpt:
A Macao court has sentenced pro-democracy ex-politician Au Kam-san to 12 years and six months in prison after a closed-door national security trial.

The ruling on Friday found 69-year-old Au guilty o...
body_text:
A Macao court has sentenced pro-democracy ex-politician Au Kam-san to 12 years and six months in prison after a closed-door national security trial.

The ruling on Friday found 69-year-old Au guilty of subverting state power by spreading false information in 2023-2024 to disrupt Macao’s 2024 leadership election.

The court said in a statement that Au also worked with “hostile organisations” abroad to spread a political agenda, and leaked confidential information to groups overseas.

“Although the defendant is a first-time offender and admitted to a considerable portion of the criminal facts, he demonstrated a high degree of intent. The degree of unlawfulness and the potential consequences of his crimes are both very serious,” the statement said.

His wife, Virginia Cheang, wrote in a public letter that the case was a political trial and a “groundless” persecution.

“From a closed-door trial to a public verdict, what kind of operation is this? It’s a political trial and it’s a groundless persecution to humiliate one’s character,” Cheang wrote.

Au’s arrest last year was the first public prosecution under Macao’s 2009 security law.

A former teacher, Au sat in the Beijing-dominated legislature for 20 years before resigning in 2021. He also helped organise Macao’s commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protest and massacre in Beijing.

Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director Maya Wang said the sentence sends a chilling message to peaceful critics and called on the European Union and Portugal to push for his release.

Macao’s government and China’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs office all backed the sentence.

This comes a day after Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, who has been imprisoned since 2020, was jailed for 10 more years under the city’s national security law.

Macao is a former Portuguese colony, which became a special administrative region of China in 1999.

title: ‘Everything is so out of whack’: UK trees experience spring six months early
excerpt:
Mild autumn temperatures causing premature flowering and raising concerns for pollinators, say experts

Trees are experiencing an “early spring” because of mild UK temperatures this autumn, with exper...
body_text:
Mild autumn temperatures causing premature flowering and raising concerns for pollinators, say experts

Trees are experiencing an “early spring” because of mild UK temperatures this autumn, with experts warning this could cause long-term harm to pollinators.

Last month was warmer than average across all parts of the UK, with October marking the ninth consecutive month with above-average mean temperatures.

Chris Nichols, the head of conservation outcomes at the Woodland Trust, said the mild weather this autumn meant horse chestnut trees were flowering and showing signs of next year’s spring growth more than six months early.

During the extreme heat this summer, many trees underwent “early autumn”, where they wilted and lost their leaves prematurely. Experts said England’s ancient oak trees were dying as a result of high temperatures and drought, as trees and ecosystems struggle to adapt fast enough to the changing climate. Scientists have said the higher than average temperatures are only possible due to the climate crisis, primarily driven by the burning of fossil fuels.

“It’s crazy, everything is so out of whack,” Nichols said, adding that the early spring was particularly concerning for pollinators.

“Trees need to flower at a certain time of year so they’re in sync with the insects. It’s like an ecological mismatch and it’s concerning in terms of the resilience of trees in the long term if they’re out of whack with the other species that they rely on,” he said.

Dr Kate Lewthwaite, a citizen science manager at the Woodland Trust, said trees flowering early was a sign of stress.

She said she suspected the drought prompted trees to shut down essential systems, similar to what happens in winter. “When the rains came, it encouraged them to start spring flowering out of season,” she said.

This, in turn, could cause the whole tree to die or be forced to resprout from dormant buds on the trunk or branches in spring, making the canopy smaller next year.

“We need to take action to help our woods and trees become more resilient to these challenges, such as rewetting woodland and slowing the flow of the rains we do get,” Lewthwaite said.

Kevin Martin, the head of tree collections at Kew Gardens, said trees in the arboretum were also going into early spring.

“The trees are all a bit confused because they’ve been so stressed this summer,” he said. “Essentially trees went into dormancy this summer and then with these warm, mild conditions they’re now going to back into growth, which means they won’t have those buds again in the spring.”

Martin said the true impact of this would not be known until spring 2028.

Earlier this summer, experts warned high winds potentially associated with El Niño could cause widespread mortality among tree species already weakened by the prolonged period of extreme heat and drought.

Martin said this impact was observed during Storm Austen and Storm Boelo, with an increase in failures compared with what would be expected during storms recording such wind speeds.

“Trees have been so stressed this year and they’ve put on very little growth, especially in the south-east where the drought has been really significant, and because of that we have, and we will see, more failures due to the storms because they’re just weakened from that stress,” he said.
