There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.

In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".

Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.

In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

Food losses are estimated in the tens of millions of euros

In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.

The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.

Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.

"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."

Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
excerpt:
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash

Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.

The L...
body_text:
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash

Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.

The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.

A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.

The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT).

"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.

The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.

Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.

"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.

"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."

Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.

Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.

In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".

They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.

An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina.

The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.

Tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson and his wife Helen Sharp with their two small children, Emma and Charlie

Robinson and Sharp's family described them as "devoted parents" and said their children were "the light of their lives".

"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," the statement read.

Robinson described himself on his LinkedIn page as the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com, and the CEO of Moltsets - all technology companies. Helen Sharp was an artist, according to media reports.

Robinson previously worked at the global financial services business Lehman Brothers and the banking group Barclays. The BBC has contacted the companies.

Anita Maria Cetina, Charmi Fehr and Rachel Reed

The joint statement also named nanny Anita Maria Cetina and said she "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family".

It added: "She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."

Rachel Reed and Charmi Fehr were described in the joint family statement as "full of joy and adventure".

"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building."

Nathalia Filgueiras received her pilot's licence when she was in high school

Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.

Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."

Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023.

"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."

A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."

He was married with two children, US media report.

Three years before crash, young copilot Nathalia Filgueiras spoke of earning a pilot licence

What Florida jet audio and flight data tells us about its final moments

Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old

title: Federal judge dismisses Trump lawsuit seeking Harvard admissions data
excerpt:
Demand for individual applicant records as part of purported civil rights review fails on procedural grounds

A federal district court judge dismissed a lawsuit on Monday filed by the Trump administra...
body_text:
Demand for individual applicant records as part of purported civil rights review fails on procedural grounds

A federal district court judge dismissed a lawsuit on Monday filed by the Trump administration seeking individual applicant records from Harvard, finding the government failed to meet procedural requirements before filing the lawsuit against the university.

Judge Myoung J Joun did not rule on the merits of the case, rather he granted a request from Harvard to dismiss the case on procedural grounds, finding that the justice department failed to demonstrate it took necessary steps to seek voluntary compliance before moving for judicial enforcement.

The justice department filed the lawsuit against Harvard in February 2026, seeking records and claiming Harvard had “thwarted” and “slow-walked” a federal civil rights review by delays and failure to meet deadlines for record requests.

The Trump administration has sought the records to ensure Harvard ceased using affirmative action in admissions.

Last week, Harvard released admissions data showing the enrollment of Black students at Harvard fell for a third straight year, to 9.3% for the class of 2030, down from 18% in the class of 2027.

“A deadline and a threat to sue, standing alone, do not necessarily demonstrate compliance with the regulatory voluntary-compliance process where the agency seeks to enforce disputed demands for extensive information,” Joun wrote in his opinion.

He also found the Department of Education failed to follow proper procedural steps prior to folding its admissions investigation into the lawsuit filed by the Department of Justice.

Harvard has maintained it provided more than 2,000 pages of documents without divulging personal individual records, which it states are privileged information. Lawyers for Harvard have argued the Trump administration prematurely abandoned negotiations with the university in favor of a retaliatory campaign against Harvard.

In August 2026, the same federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard, in one of the Trump administration’s many efforts against Harvard that has included freezing federal funds and attempting to revoke Harvard’s ability to accept international students.

title: Trump says that US will stop paying Israel aid after year-end
excerpt:
US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump says he made a deal with ⁠Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that ⁠Washington would no longer be providing funding to Israel after the end of this ‌year.

“Now, as f...
body_text:
US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump says he made a deal with ⁠Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that ⁠Washington would no longer be providing funding to Israel after the end of this ‌year.

“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn ⁠a year, and ⁠we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” Trump told ⁠Fox News’ Fox and Friends after voting in the midterm elections began.

“We’ve ⁠already agreed that ⁠by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. ‌Now we’ll help Israel if they need it.”

It was not immediately clear what form of aid Trump was discussing.

Military aid to Israel, and US political campaign contributions from Israel’s backers to candidates, have been a flashpoint for both Democrats and Republicans this year.

Harsh public criticism of Israel by US political leaders in recent years marks a dramatic shift from decades of staunch bipartisan backing.

The US House of Representatives defeated an amendment to cut off aid to Israel in July, despite nearly half of Democrats supporting it, reflecting a growing rupture between US progressives and Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.

The House voted 314 to ‌104 to defeat the measure, offered as an amendment to a State Department spending bill by outgoing Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, an outspoken Republican critic of US policy in the Middle East.

title: Car finance: Barclays becomes first big lender to offer payouts for mis-selling of loans
excerpt:
Bank to make ‘early settlement’ offers before outcome of legal battle, with those who accept likely to get money before Christmas

Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thous...
body_text:
Bank to make ‘early settlement’ offers before outcome of legal battle, with those who accept likely to get money before Christmas

Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thousands of people who claim they were mis-sold car loans, with some of those who accept likely to see the money land in their account before Christmas.

Amid an ongoing legal battle over an industry-wide compensation scheme for victims of the UK’s car finance scandal, Barclays has become the first big UK lender to break cover and begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained.

Under the rules, “early settlement” offers of this kind must at least match what people would receive under the multibillion-pound scheme that is being challenged – which may help to address fears that banks might try to make “lowball” offers.

But consumers face a tricky decision as, depending on the outcome of the legal battle, they could end up with more money, less money or nothing at all if they decide to decline the offer and wait.

In March this year, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a £9.1bn compensation scheme for the millions of victims of the scandal.

But legal challenges forced the regulator to partly suspend the scheme, and a hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February next year.

The FCA had expected to start paying out £829 on average this year to those affected by the scandal, in which drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers between 2007 and 2024.

Millions of people were treated unfairly when they took out motor finance to buy a new or secondhand car, motorbike or van, and ended up paying more than they should have done.

Until the legal challenge is concluded, lenders do not need to pay compensation to people owed money under the scheme.

However, Barclays Partner Finance – part of the banking group – has decided to offer payments now to some of those who would be due compensation under the scheme.

That has prompted speculation that other companies on the hook for payouts will follow suit.

It is understood that over the next couple of weeks, tens of thousands of Barclays customers who have already complained will be contacted directly and offered “an early full and final settlement”.

Barclays is using the FCA model to calculate the compensation offers. It said: “Acceptance is optional, and customers will receive clear information on how their offer has been calculated and what accepting it would mean.”

They will have a month to accept or reject the offer, and if they say yes, the bank will pay the money into their designated account. It is thought the first payments for those who accept the offer will arrive before Christmas – which may feed into some people’s decision-making.

But those who accept cannot then later seek additional compensation or pursue further complaints or legal claims relating to the commission on that agreement.

Alternatively, people can reject the offer and wait to see what happens. The FCA said that if it saw off the legal challenge and its scheme was upheld, payments could begin in 2027, but if the judgment was appealed or the scheme was partially or wholly overturned, any compensation owed could be delayed until 2028 or later.

Ultimately, depending on the outcome, those who decline the early offers could end up being entitled to “more, less, or no compensation”, the regulator said. It added that it supported lenders making settlement offers, “as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme”.

Barclays Partner Finance said it would not ask people who accept now to repay any of their compensation if the final outcome meant they would have been entitled to less cash.

Barclays has set aside £430m in connection with alleged motor finance mis-selling, and it is not clear how many people could be affected in total, or what proportion will receive early settlement offers.

Under the FCA scheme as it currently stands, compensation payments depend on the details of the case.

By far the biggest category is deals that allowed the dealer or broker to increase the interest rate the customer would pay, to get a higher commission.

title: Iran commander sets out five conditions for regional security
excerpt: The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces has laid out five conditions for what he calls a roadmap to lasting security, as Qatar said it was “hopeful” that Tehran and Washington could reach a deal pav...
body_text:
The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces has laid out five conditions for what he calls a roadmap to lasting security, as Qatar said it was “hopeful” that Tehran and Washington could reach a deal paving the way for future negotiations, despite overnight US strikes on Qeshm Island.

Major-General Ali Abdollahi’s plan calls for an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, the complete lifting of sanctions and the unfreezing of Iranian assets and war reparations, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported on Tuesday.

The plan also calls for recognition of Iran’s sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, and a guarantee against future aggression under a regional security framework for West Asia.

The plan comes as Qatar steps up mediation efforts amid fears the US-Israel war on Iran, launched in late February, could escalate after the midterm elections in the United States on Tuesday.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Majed al-Ansari said in his weekly briefing in Doha on Tuesday that a Qatari delegation held a meeting with Iranian officials in Tehran for more than three hours on Monday, before returning to Doha that evening. Both sides are now reviewing Qatar’s proposal, he said, with mediators exchanging proposals between them in real time.

“If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations,” al-Ansari said, adding that Qatar would not speculate on whether an agreement or a military escalation was more likely.

He warned that any escalation, whether attacks on Iranian territory or on shipping, “will have an impact on the negotiations”, and said continuing the Qatari-Pakistani mediation remained a priority. He reiterated that freedom of navigation in Hormuz was nonnegotiable, referring to Doha’s condemnation of the targeting of the Qatari tanker Al-Mayda.

Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas said mediators were aiming to avert a new round of fighting.

He said a Qatari delegation visited Iran on Friday in response to a letter to Iran from US Vice President JD Vance, and an Iranian delegation travelled to Qatar the following day.

“The Qataris are trying to mediate with Iran, not on a peace deal, but on a framework to restart the negotiations,” he said. Of Monday’s brief visit, he added: “The reading is that the Qataris carried a message to Tehran and immediately left after that.”

“The main issue is the mistrust between the two parties,” Atas said. “The Iranians say that twice previously the US attacked them when they were engaged in diplomacy. That’s why they’re asking for concrete steps, such as lifting sanctions, removing the naval blockade, returning frozen Iranian assets and letting Iran sell oil on the global market.”

US officials reportedly said the military carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island on Monday that did not amount to a resumption of major combat operations, saying Iran had tried to target a US aircraft and the attack took out the launcher.

One official called it “a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”. IRNA reported five explosions on the island, with more blasts heard in Bandar Lengeh. President Donald Trump had said on October 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday it downed two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the strait.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s lead negotiator, said, “The ball is in America’s court to prevent war.”

Tehran’s Hamshahri newspaper reported that Iran had updated its target bank to include US bases and infrastructure in Europe.

Zeidon Alkinani, the founding director of the Arab Perceptions Institute, said both sides remained open to diplomacy.

“Diplomacy and force are running in parallel,” Alkinani told Al Jazeera. “The diplomatic channel is alive – it has always been since March, but there hasn’t unfortunately been a fundamental breakthrough.”

Vance had said on Monday he was optimistic about reaching a negotiated settlement.

However, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday Iran was neither waiting for the outcome of US midterm elections nor shaping its policies around them.

title: Saudi Pro League postpones matches after Asian Cup rescheduling
excerpt:
Matches in Saudi Arabia’s premier football league scheduled for the coming week have been postponed after the rescheduling of the AFC Asian Cup 2027, the Saudi Pro League (SPL) says.

“The decision co...
body_text:
Matches in Saudi Arabia’s premier football league scheduled for the coming week have been postponed after the rescheduling of the AFC Asian Cup 2027, the Saudi Pro League (SPL) says.

“The decision comes as part of a wider review of the ⁠⁠2026-27 league ⁠⁠fixture schedule, with the revised Asian Cup dates creating additional flexibility in the domestic football calendar,” the SPL said ⁠⁠in a statement on Tuesday, two days before the start of the match week.

The postponement of the Asian Cup until December next year was announced earlier in the day after recent attacks on the kingdom. The 24-team continental tournament had been due to take place from January 7 to February 5.

Asian football’s governing body announced the decision after “extensive discussions and close consultation with the Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the AFC Asian Cup Saudi Arabia 2027 and the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF)”.

The tournament will now run from December 23, 2027, to January 21, 2028.

An attack on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 13 ‌‌people and wounded more than 300. Yemen’s Houthis  claimed responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Further attacks on the airport in the span of a week killed at least five more people.

“New ⁠⁠dates for matchweek 13 ⁠⁠will be announced once the review is complete.”

The SPL has rescheduled several domestic league games this season for logistical ‌‌reasons, and last month’s AFC Champions League Elite clash in Riyadh between hosts Al-Nassr and Emirati ‌‌side ‌‌Al Wasl was postponed due to a threat of missile attacks.

Kickoff was delayed after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued a safety warning 15 minutes before ⁠⁠the scheduled start time.

title: Judge orders Iowa to permit Satanic Temple holiday event at state capitol
excerpt:
Federal court says group likely to win its free speech claim and tells officials to approve application within seven days

A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit a local S...
body_text:
Federal court says group likely to win its free speech claim and tells officials to approve application within seven days

A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit a local Satanic Temple organization to hold a holiday event in the rotunda of the state capitol after years of denying the group’s application.

The religious organization and Iowa Republican state officials have been in a legal battle over the group’s applications to hold a holiday event at the state capitol in recent years.

Republicans in Iowa, who currently control the governorship and majorities in the state house and senate, have cited the capitol building’s policies prohibiting gratuitous violence and obscene displays as justification for denying the applications.

According to the office of the attorney general, Brenna Bird, state Republicans intend to appeal the federal judge’s decision.

The Satanic Temple and Iowa chapter leader filed a lawsuit in August, alleging discrimination from former and current state officials.

Chief District Judge Stephanie M Rose stated in her court order that the group was likely to succeed on its free speech claim and ordered the current director of the Iowa department of administrative services to approve the holiday event application within seven days.

The Satanic Temple (TST), which was founded in Salem, Massachusetts, in 2013, characterizes itself as a “non-theistic religious organization” that advocates for secularism and emphasizes separation from the Church of Satan founded in 1966.

In December 2023, the group had a religious holiday display in the Iowa state capitol, but it was vandalized by a Christian military veteran. The Turning Point founder, Charlie Kirk, pledged $10,000 to the accused vandal’s legal defense. The following year, the Satanic Temple’s application for a holiday display and event was denied.

“State officials have made it clear that they denied TST permission to hold events in the Capitol rotunda because they disagreed with their religious viewpoint,” said Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, in a statement on the court order. “It is a foundational principle that the government cannot restrict speech in this way, favor one religion over another, or discriminate against religious groups because they don’t agree with them.”

The group said its proposed holiday event would include costumes of the European folklore character Krampus, caroling, coloring for children and ornament making. In its denial of the application, state officials cited sticks included in the costumes that could be used as weapons and policies meant to protect children who might be present in the public space.

Judge Rose wrote that the state officials’ arguments did not justify the denials, noting the argument that the character Krampus might scare children was “not a permissible basis for excluding speech” and the argument about the sticks included with the costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event”.

The Iowa department of administrative services and the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, have not yet commented on the court order.

In 2023, Governor Reynolds stated in response to the group’s holiday display at the state capitol, “like many Iowans, I find the Satanic Temple’s display in the Capitol absolutely objectionable. In a free society, the best response to objectionable speech is more speech, and I encourage all those of faith to join me today in praying over the Capitol and recognizing the nativity scene that will be on display – the true reason for the season.”

title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
excerpt:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region

China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomati...
body_text:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region

China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.

The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.

Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.

President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.

Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.

He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”

Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.

When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.

Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”

As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.

Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.

China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.

According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.

The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.

Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.

Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.

Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

title: RBA interest rates: Bullock says ‘some pain now’ will prevent worse pain later as Reserve Bank hikes rates for fifth time
excerpt:
Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008

RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank cash rate decision

Get our daily political emai...
body_text:
Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008

RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank cash rate decision

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has said that “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” after lifting official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation.

The RBA’s decision to hit mortgage holders for a fifth time in 2026 will intensify pressure on indebted households, but signals from the central bank suggest policymakers may now wait to gauge the full economic fallout before pulling the trigger again.

The decision split the monetary policy board, with six members voting for a hike, while three were in favour of holding the cash rate steady.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Bullock told journalists shortly after the rate decision that inflation needed to come down “and we will do what is necessary to achieve that”.

In its post meeting statement, the RBA did not include an explicit reference to the potential need for further hikes, signalling the RBA is now prepared to wait and see the effects of this year’s multiple rate rises.

Economists from major investment houses, including UBS, understood the change in language from past statements to be “clearly dovish”, signalling the likelihood that rates would remain were they are at least in the short term.

The cash rate is now at its highest level since 2008.

The back-to-back hikes will heap more pain on over 3.3m households with home loans and turn the screws on a federal government under pressure for its economic management.

The latest rate rise will lift the monthly interest payment on a $700,000 home loan by $107, according to Canstar, bringing the total rise in repayments over this year’s five hikes to $532.

Bullock said on Tuesday that while the rate rise, which informs mortgages, is not the news that many Australians want to hear, “it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.

“Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” Bullock said.

As the central bank struggles to explain to Australians how interest rate hikes will help tame inflation made worse by events overseas, the RBA’s latest set of forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy (SOMP) showed a difficult period ahead for the economy.

The forecasts showed the country’s cost of living crisis would extend for another year, even as Australia struggles with below trend economic growth and climbing unemployment.

The 4.3% inflation rate in the year to September was substantially stronger than the RBA had anticipated as a worsening Middle East conflict squashed hopes of a quick resolution to the global oil shock.

Inflation will push higher through the final months of 2026 and only return below 3% – within the bank’s 2 to 3% target range – by the end of next year, or about nine months later than hoped, the latest forecasts showed.

Amid a heated political stoush over whether the federal government’s spending is to blame for high and rising inflation, the RBA noted in its SOMP that public demand was weaker than expected through the first six months of 2026.

That was the result of cost of living measures rolling off and “moderating” spending in areas such as defence and disability and aged care services, the SOMP said.

Global oil prices would ease over the coming 18 months, but still remain relatively elevated, according to the forecasts, suggesting limited relief from high fuel costs for motorists and ongoing high costs for businesses.

“We view the risks to the inflation outlook as still skewed to the upside,” the report said.

Alongside persistent cost of living pressures, the RBA also predicted weak economic growth through to the end of 2028.

The economy would grow by 1.6% this year and by 1.3% in 2027.

That would be well below an estimated potential growth rate of about 2%, but better than recent forecasts by bank analysts.

And despite the risks associated with a housing downturn that “is one of the steepest over the past 50 years”, the central banks’ economists saw no evidence that the country was headed towards recession over the coming two years.

Unemployment, now at 4.7%, would end next year at about 4.9%, before creeping over 5% in 2028. Importantly, employment would remain positive.

Meanwhile, there was no end in sight for the global artificial intelligence boom, which would continue to add to capacity issues in Australia.

The RBA nearly tripled its forecast for business investment growth in 2026 to 12%.

title: RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank of Australia announces cash rate hike to 4.85% after meeting today – latest news
excerpt:
Reserve Bank raises interest rates to an 18-year high in fifth hike this year

Full report: RBA hikes cash rate for fifth time this year in blow to mortgage holders

Use our loan calculator to check h...
body_text:
Reserve Bank raises interest rates to an 18-year high in fifth hike this year

Full report: RBA hikes cash rate for fifth time this year in blow to mortgage holders

Use our loan calculator to check how the rate rise may affect you

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Bullock says she doesn’t “see the economy cracking at this point” even though some people will feel like they are experiencing a recession.

The decision to raise interest rates for a fifth time this year will face inevitable accusations the RBA is pushing the country into an economic downturn.

Bullock pushes back against that framing:

double quotation markOur central forecasts do not see us going into recession, but it does see growth slowing quite markedly.

It shows that consumption is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer, their spending can’t grow very quickly because their incomes aren’t growing very quickly.

Tim Wilson rejects Gallagher’s blaming of parliament for lack 0f savings policy

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, has rejected Katy Gallagher’s accusation that parliament is to blame for the lack of spending-saving policies.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, he said:

double quotation markWe wrote to the government at the start of the year and said: let’s have a bipartisan approach to reducing government spending. The government rejected that.

Every time we have asked them to audit government expenditure to see if it is financing organised crime, they have rejected that.

Wilson said he does not believe the government is committed to delivering net savings.

double quotation markThey will never commit to that because, as we know and history shows, for every $2 of savings they claim to find, they go on and spend another $3, and it ends up only stoking inflation further.

Katy Gallagher says parliament to blame for lack of government savings

The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, has blamed the parliament for blocking the government’s attempts to introduce spending-saving policies.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, the Labor minister said:

double quotation markI hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending. I don’t hear as many specifics about where people would like to see that come from.

In fact, we’ve got savings in the parliament now that the parliament is refusing to pass.

Asked whether the government intends to deliver net savings in the next budget, Gallagher said:

double quotation markWe’ll be making responsible savings decisions, in line with the job we have to do. I say, in the last two updates, our policy decisions line has contributed positively to the budget overall. That shows you the approach that Jim [Chalmers] and I have taken, and we’ll continue to bring that approach to the decisions we’ve got over the next few weeks as we finalise them.

It’s not unusual for a finance minister, or a treasurer, or a prime minister to have an ambitious appetite around savings, but we need to work through our processes respectfully.

Bullock says she doesn’t “see the economy cracking at this point” even though some people will feel like they are experiencing a recession.

The decision to raise interest rates for a fifth time this year will face inevitable accusations the RBA is pushing the country into an economic downturn.

Bullock pushes back against that framing:

double quotation markOur central forecasts do not see us going into recession, but it does see growth slowing quite markedly.

It shows that consumption is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer, their spending can’t grow very quickly because their incomes aren’t growing very quickly.

The Australian stock market ended higher after the central bank did what it was expected to do and hiked interest rates for the fifth time this calendar year.

The main S&P/ASX200 index rose 30.3 points, or 0.3%, to 8886.8, as the broader All Ordinaries gained 31.7 points, or 0.4%, to 9008.9.

Most of the market’s 11 sectors were in the green, with the major materials and consumer stocks leading the way, while the energy sector carried most of the loss-makers.

The Reserve Bank board ended its two-day meeting on monetary policy on Tuesday with a 25 basis point rise in the cash interest rate to 4.85%.

The Australian dollar was buying 69.77 US cents, down from 70.21 US cents at 5pm on Monday.

Bullock asked about effect of US-Israel war in Iran on interest rates

Guardian Australia’s economics editor, Patrick Commins, asks Bullock whether the RBA would have raised rates if oil prices had stayed low.

In other words, what would have happened had the US and Israel not launched strikes against Iran?

Bullock gives a nuanced response, pointing out that Australia already had a problem with “excess demand” that required cooling.

double quotation markNow, would that have meant that we had to go up the same amount? I don’t know the answer to that.

It’s possible that it’s caused interest rates to mean they have to be a little bit higher.

Bullock goes on to articulate an economic risk posed by raising inflation expectations caused by high oil prices: as consumers resign themselves to higher prices, businesses lift theirs ahead of anticipated rising costs, creating a self-fulfilling loop that entrenches inflation.

RBA independence from government ‘a two-way street’, Bullock says

Michele Bullock has described independence as a “two-way street”, noting that she doesn’t tell the government what to spend on, and that the government doesn’t tell the RBA what to do with rates.

The role of public sector spending in fuelling inflation looms large, with Labor under pressure from critics over five rate hikes this year.

Bullock says that governments need to decide on how much spending is required to provide for the nation. She says:

double quotation markBut that is for governments to decide. Independence is a two-way street. I don’t tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don’t tell me what to do with interest rates.

Unemployment and housing concerns behind board split: RBA governor

More from Michele Bullock’s press conference:

The RBA decision to raise rates was split, with three members of the rate-setting board preferring a hold, while six voted to raise.

Bullock says those in favour of a hold were concerned about risks to the economy, including rising unemployment and housing weakness. Bullock said:

double quotation markThey felt that there were potential downside risks in these circumstances, particularly since we’d already done four interest rate rises, and maybe we should wait a bit longer to get some more data to test that.

Bullock says market watchers shouldn’t interpret the split decision as a sign the RBA won’t raise further if inflation risks materialise.

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, says “this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.

She says “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”.

double quotation markI understand that today’s decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments.

But households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough. Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance, and other essentials.

High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on.

The comments were made in opening remarks to journalists in Sydney ahead of questions.

Several economists are interpreting the RBA’s statement accompanying the rate hike as “dovish”, which means further hikes are less likely.

UBS economists describe the decision as “clearly dovish” while Anthony Malouf, economist at Ebury, says there is an “absence of a clear tightening bias”.

The Australian dollar also immediately dropped against its US counterpart after the decision, which shows traders do not believe the central bank is, at this stage, looking to hike much further.

This could all change if inflation remains elevated, but for the moment, some economists and currency traders believe this could be the last hike, at least for a while.

Chalmers was asked about the federal budget and its impact on inflation. He said:

double quotation markOur budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role and that’s what we intend to do.

He was also asked if he’d consider stepping aside.

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, is speaking now after the RBA’s decision. He said:

double quotation markToday’s decision was widely expected, but that doesn’t make it any easier for Australian families and businesses to absorb. It will be difficult news for many Australians who are already paying a hefty price for circumstances outside of their control.

He pointed to the ongoing war in the Middle East as a major factor in inflation:

double quotation markThe war’s in its ninth month and its re-escalation is putting sustained upward pressure on inflation.

It’s weighing on growth and its end can’t come soon enough for the global economy or for Australians facing cost of living pressures.

Macquarie Bank announces it will pass rate rise on

Macquarie Bank has already announced it will pass on the interest rate rise to mortgage holders.

The bank said it will increase variable home loans by 0.25%, effective 19 November. It will also increase ongoing variable rates paid on its transactions and savings accounts by 0.25%, a boon to savers. Ben Perham, the head of personal banking, said:

double quotation markWith household budgets already feeling the strain, today’s decision by the RBA will be challenging for many Australians.

To help our variable home loan customers prepare, we’re again waiting more than two weeks before this latest increase takes effect.

The cash rate is now the highest it has been in 18 years

The decision was not a unanimous one: six members of the RBA board voted to raise the cash rate, while three voted to leave it unchanged.

double quotation markThe Board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high. Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target.

The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target.

title: Judge pauses Alan Jones indecent assault trial so former broadcaster can watch Melbourne Cup
excerpt:
Jones, a former radio broadcaster, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The evidence of a star rep...
body_text:
Jones, a former radio broadcaster, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The evidence of a star reporter whose investigation led to charges against Alan Jones was paused so the former 2GB broadcaster and horse racing enthusiast could watch the Melbourne Cup.

Jones’s defence barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, asked judge Glenn Walsh if the court could break just before 3pm to watch the race as Jones sat laughing loudly in the front row of the public gallery.

Walsh smiled as he said he knew there was “a particular race” the defendant would be interested in and agreed to break from 2.50pm until 3.10pm. The court commonly will adjourn mid-afternoon to give witnesses a short break.

The Sydney Morning Herald’s chief investigative reporter, Kate McClymont, was in the witness box all day answering questions about her years-long investigation of Jones which was published in 2023.

Under cross-examination by Bashir, McClymont agreed that she used the expression “go the grope” in her interview with complainant C, but said the alleged victim had repeated the phrase.

“You’re not looking for sexy phrases to put in a story, you’re having a conversation with someone,” she said.

McClymont told the court that readership and advertising metrics were of no relevance to her as a journalist. She had been asked if “special investigations under your name sell newspapers”.

Bashir took the witness to call logs and emails between her and her colleagues, including columnist Peter FitzSimons and reporter Jennifer Duke dating back to 2017.

After speaking to a man who made allegations about Jones, known as complainant C in the trial, McClymont wrote: “We have another one.”

In her opening statement Bashir said McClymont and FitzSimons were “looking for a story” and their reporting was fuelled by the hatred and jealousy of his 2GB radio rival Ray Hadley.

McClymont said FitzSimons had been working on a story about allegations against Jones since October 2017 and it was a “long-running matter”.

Earlier, McClymont said the three alleged victims of Jones that she interviewed received no benefit from her or the media company for telling their stories.

McClymont, whose articles led to other alleged victims coming forward, is giving evidence in the lengthy trial of the former broadcaster, who is facing 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching against five men.

Several men detailed claims of indecent assault against Jones in McClymont’s articles, including that he groped or inappropriately touched them without their consent.

Police say they formed Strike Force Bonnefin after McClymont’s reporting in the Herald and the Age resulted in alleged victims coming forward.

At the Downing Centre local court on Tuesday, Jones, 85, was supported by men’s rights activist Bettina Arndt and defamation lawyer Paul Svilans from Mark O’Brien Legal.

McClymont, who has won 10 Walkley awards for excellence in journalism, was supported by the editor of the SMH, Jordan Baker, and the deputy editor, Nick Ralston.

McClymont told the court she always sought comment from Jones and his legal team before publication via text and email. In her evidence she agreed with prosecutor Georgina Wright that she spoke to three alleged victims but kept their stories confidential from each other.

McClymont did not initially share her interview notes or recordings with police because they were confidential or not available but received a subpoena for the material in 2026, the court heard.

The strike force was formed after the December 2023 publication of McClymont’s years-long investigation of Jones.

His long radio career came to an abrupt end in 2020 after a series of on-air incidents led to the radio station losing advertisers and haemorrhaging revenue.

When Jones was arrested by New South Wales police after a “long, thorough, protracted” investigation at his city apartment in late 2024, he had been retired from his $4m-a-year breakfast radio show on 2GB for four years.

title: ‘A serious failure’: CPS prosecutor cites imaginary case to high court after AI search
excerpt:
Exclusive: Nonexistent precedent cited in alleged child rape case adds to dozens of AI-related errors plaguing court proceedings

A senior crown prosecutor acting in a high court case cited an imagina...
body_text:
Exclusive: Nonexistent precedent cited in alleged child rape case adds to dozens of AI-related errors plaguing court proceedings

A senior crown prosecutor acting in a high court case cited an imaginary legal precedent in an error that has sparked fresh concerns about AI hallucinations infecting the justice system.

Ravinder Dhillon, representing the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), referenced an entirely made-up case during a dispute over whether a child should be prosecuted for the rape of his younger sister, court documents have revealed.

Her explanation for how the nonexistent case came to be relied on has been called “unsatisfactory” by two senior high court judges and a “serious failure” by an expert in AI and law. The Guardian understands the reference came from an AI response generated during an internet search.

The case adds to dozens of others where AI-related errors have plagued court proceedings this year, mostly from people who are not legally qualified representing themselves, and often in employment tribunal cases.

It is only the second known case involving the CPS – the main public agency bringing criminal prosecutions in England and Wales – which admitted in February that one of its lawyers acting in an extradition case involving two Romanians convicted of minor offences cited nonexistent legal authorities, likely caused by AI. Those made-up cases were only spotted when opposition lawyers could find no trace of them and the CPS concluded “the risk of recurrence was low”.

In the latest case, lawyers for the boy, who was 11 at the time of the alleged rape of his seven-year-old sister, were challenging the CPS’s decision to prosecute him. They alleged prosecutors had failed to take into account representations from social workers, youth workers and a forensic psychologist. Dhillon, a senior crown prosecutor in the CPS’s rape and serious sexual offences unit, was arguing in favour of the prosecution of the child and submitted a detailed reference to a case she called CPS – R v J [2024] EWCA Crim 3529. It turned out not to exist.

The decision to proceed was taken by Dhillon in April and confirmed by the chief crown prosecutor. Then in October Dhillon admitted that the nonexistent citation had been made in error. She said she had been referring to a completely different decision – this time a real one – that was made 15 years earlier.

“This was used as a legal source to argue for the prosecution of a child and that legal source doesn’t exist: that’s a serious failure,” said Brian Flanagan, associate professor of law at Maynooth University in Ireland who investigates the use of AI by judges. “It calls into question norms of trust in the law where we treat authorities as precious things. You can’t make them up; it’s out of bounds. AI increases the risk that is going to happen because of the time you can save. It is not great for any professional to do this, but when the professional is working for the state it takes on a different aspect, because the power of the state is immense.”

The high court said the CPS’s reference to a fictitious case did not affect the outcome of the boy’s challenge to the decision to continue with his prosecution, which is listed to go to trial in the youth courts later this week.

In June 2025, the high court responded to AI hallucinations in cases spanning housing to banking, by calling on the Bar Council and the Law Society to consider steps to curb the problem “as a matter of urgency”. Dame Victoria Sharp, then president of the King’s bench division, warned of “serious implications for the administration of justice and public confidence in the justice system if artificial intelligence is misused” and said lawyers misusing AI could face sanctions, from public admonishment to contempt of court proceedings and referral to the police.

Asked for comment, the CPS said it has a strict AI policy “which limits its use so that it is not used to make legal decisions and there must be human checks for accuracy”.

A spokesperson said the CPS “identified an error had occurred from conducting legal research using the internet”.

“As soon as this error was identified, it was remedied and an internal review was carried out to establish how this had occurred and to check that no other cases have been affected,” they said. “Following the rapid review we shared learnings, including that case law must be cited from trusted legal sources.”

It is understood the internet search delivered an AI summary which contained the fictional case details.

The latest incident brings to 101 the number of entries in a UK tracker maintained by Doughty Street Chambers barrister Matthew Lee covering confirmed, suspected and disputed AI-related errors, as well as related false citations. He said the cases identified may be the “tip of the iceberg”, as many lower court decisions are never published.

He added there are privacy and confidentiality risks associated with the CPS using AI, given the highly sensitive information it handles, and warned that AI was creating additional work for barristers, who need to spend time checking the authenticity of legal authorities appearing in case papers where AI may have been used in their preparation.

title: Denmark pushes for EU ban on ‘turbo chickens’ as secret footage causes outrage
excerpt:
Minister says government will work towards banning fast-growing breed across country and throughout EU

The Danish government is pursuing a national ban on “turbo chickens” and is calling for the fast...
body_text:
Minister says government will work towards banning fast-growing breed across country and throughout EU

The Danish government is pursuing a national ban on “turbo chickens” and is calling for the fast-growing breed to be prohibited across Europe.

The move comes amid widespread outrage over allegations of lawbreaking by one of Denmark’s big chicken producers.

According to a TV2 documentary broadcast last week, producer Christian Tvergaard broke Danish law by giving chickens only half the amount of darkness per day that is required, in order to encourage them to eat more. The documentary featured secretly filmed footage from a chicken coop in North Jutland.

The Ross 308 breed, labelled the turbo chicken, is the most widespread in Danish poultry production. It grows from about 50 grams to 2kg in just 33 days. Such rapid growth can lead to problems with the animal’s bones and organs. Other chicken breeds take between 46 and 63 days to reach the same weight.

Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare, Christian Rabjerg Madsen, said he discouraged Danes from buying turbo chickens, telling the broadcaster: “I want to work for a national ban. But it’s clear that this is something that needs to be investigated both legally and economically.”

He added: “Now we will work for a national ban, we will work for a ban at EU level.”

In response to the documentary, Tvergaard has admitted to making some wrong decisions.

He told TV2: “I look inward and must admit that I have made some wrong decisions. There is no excuse for that, but I can learn from it and correct where I have not done well enough.

“And I have done that, both when it comes to the lighting programme and a number of the workflows we have in the stable, where both procedures and the roster have been tightened up.”

The proposal for the ban on turbo chickens is gaining political momentum and attracting cross-party support in Denmark. But industry figures warn that to be effective, any ban must include imported chickens as well.

Klement Hinkbøl Ribergaard, the chief executive of chicken producer Danpo, said: “If Denmark alone bans the production of fast-growing chickens while shops, restaurants and consumers in the Danish market can continue to buy imported, fast-growing chicken of more or less questionable quality, we risk a situation in which animal welfare certainly does not benefit.”

With fast-growing breeds so prominent across the EU, it would mark a landmark shift. According to Eurogroup for Animals, 95% of chickens in the bloc are now raised in intensive systems and bred to produce the cheapest amount of meat possible, creating a “race to the bottom”.

“Fast-growing breeds are inherently predisposed to suffering, with their bodies growing so quickly they can barely stand on their legs,” said Reineke Hameleers, the advocacy group’s chief executive. “Denmark’s political willingness to stop this is an example that should be followed by the EU, for it presents the progressiveness this industry needs, one that is backed up by scientific evidence.”

Britta Riis, chief executive of Animal Protection Denmark, said turbo chickens were the result of a “deeply unethical and grotesque form of breeding” that led to “systematic abuse” and considerable suffering for the birds. The organisation is calling for all chickens to be bred for the same amount of time as organic breeds, which is 56 days.

Animal welfare has featured heavily in public debate in recent months in Denmark. The issue of pig farming dominated the last general election to such an extent that it was nicknamed the “pig election”.

The country is due to stop mink farming by August 2029 after the current government decided not to seek an EU exemption on the practice.

title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying
excerpt:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to eng...
body_text:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.

This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.

Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.

Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool, where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.

But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.

A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.

Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.

During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.

After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.

When Reynolds asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.

The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.

A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.

After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.

“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.

Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024, which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.

A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: New York child dies from measles in state’s first fatal case in 30 years
excerpt:
New York governor says case is ‘devastating reminder of what’s at stake’ when vaccine protections are eroded

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s...
body_text:
New York governor says case is ‘devastating reminder of what’s at stake’ when vaccine protections are eroded

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced on Monday.

The child died in Lewis county, about 93 miles (150km) north of Syracuse, New York governor Kathy Hochul said.

“I am heartbroken to learn that a child in Lewis County has died after contracting measles,” Hochul said in a statement.

Hochul linked the death to the federal government’s stance on immunisation, saying: “This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”

Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. Although rare, deaths from measles occur in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases.

The US stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the US this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported six deaths this year.

Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring states and in rural areas of New York.

The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of late October – more than double the tally for 2025.

Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US department of health and human services (HHS), has faced criticism for his comments on some vaccines, and made sweeping changes to vaccination policy, including cutting childhood immunisation recommendations by a third.

title: Peacock found in couple’s Brisbane bathroom leads to creative bid to reunite bird with tattoo artist
excerpt:
Geoff and Delwyn Ballantyne went out for an evening coffee. When they returned they found Hex admiring himself in the mirror

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A peacock tha...
body_text:
Geoff and Delwyn Ballantyne went out for an evening coffee. When they returned they found Hex admiring himself in the mirror

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A peacock that seemingly fell hopelessly in love with himself in a bathroom mirror after breaking into a Brisbane house remains on the run after being evicted.

Geoff and Delwyn Ballantyne left their Alexandra Hills home last week for an evening coffee and returned to find a fully grown peacock gazing adoringly at himself in their bathroom mirror.

“We … assume the bird was in the front yard and, as we opened the garage door, he must have walked in,” Geoff said. “Because when we got in, there he was, admiring himself.”

Delwyn was the first to spot the bird and responded with alarm.

“There was a lot of screaming from my wife. She thought there must have been an intruder but then she says it’s a peacock,” Geoff said. “I did believe her, but I tried not to, because it wasn’t very believable.”

The couple attempted to break the visitor’s steadfast gazing into the mirror by offering it water and crackers. When that failed, wildlife rescuers were called in.

They wrangled the peacock into a towel then released it into nearby bushland. Since then the bird been paying afternoon visits to Suzie Tafolo’s acreage home – also in Alexandra Hills.

Tafolo suspected the bird might have belonged to a local tattoo artist, Elliot Ross, who was looking for his missing peacock, Hex. Ross subsequently confirmed the bird in the Ballantynes’ bathroom and at Tafolo’s property was Hex, due to his unusual plumage.

“I’ve Googled how to catch a peacock, which is something I never thought I’d have to do,” Tafolo said on Monday. “One of the things it says is that they love mirrors, which makes sense in terms of how he ended up in the bathroom.”

Tafolo carted a full-length mirror from her house to the back shed where Hex has been turning up each day.

Hex appeared to take an interest in his reflection on Tuesday and Tafolo said she was hopeful he could soon be reunited with Ross who has owned the bird for a couple of years.

“This is the first time he’s gone walkabout besides going into our neighbour’s property,” Ross said.

“We’ve got a female here as well and she’s stayed. I’m guessing he’s gone walkabout trying to find another female. We’re hoping to try to catch him.”

Griffith University professor emeritus Darryl Jones, an urban ecologist and author of Wild Neighbours, has studied how birds respond to their reflections.

He believes Hex might have been lonely – but not necessarily looking for love.

“Most birds would see it as a rival or a threat or something like that, and usually fight it. But this bird might be just lonely,” he said.

“It’s pretty unusual for two males to be hanging out together, but they will sometimes. Peacocks are not that smart. He might be dumb – but he knows what a female looks like.”

title: ‘Going hungry’: Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs
excerpt:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – Laili Begum can no longer afford to keep her two children in school. There are days when the 37-year-old garment worker struggles to put even one proper meal on the table.

An expe...
body_text:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – Laili Begum can no longer afford to keep her two children in school. There are days when the 37-year-old garment worker struggles to put even one proper meal on the table.

An experienced sewing operator at Virtual Bottoms Limited, a ready-made garments factory near Bangladesh’s capital Dhaka, Begum earns around 15,000 taka ($121) a month, which sometimes rises to 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161) when she works overtime.

Her 15-year-old daughter and 12-year-old son dropped out of school earlier this year because she could not afford their education.

“We can barely afford one proper meal a day. This morning, we had only puffed rice and Bombay mix [a snack]. There was nothing for lunch. We’ve been going hungry, hoping to have a proper meal tonight. Yesterday was the same. This is how we survive now,” she told Al Jazeera.

“My son is so thin that you can count every rib in his chest. What else can I do?”

Begum is among approximately four million garment factory workers in Bangladesh, half of them women. They are now protesting for better wages.

Bangladesh, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, is a key supplier to global fashion brands such as H&M, Zara, Levi Strauss, Walmart, and Primark. The country’s ready-made garment sector accounts for more ⁠than 80 percent of its export earnings, which touched $39bn last financial year.

Yet, the people sewing those clothes say their pay no longer covers basic living costs.

A Muslim-majority South Asian nation of 170 million people, Bangladesh has one of the world’s lowest wages among apparel-producing countries.

Cambodia has a minimum wage of $210 a month for garment workers, Vietnam’s range from $140-$210, while wages at China’s manufacturing hub of Guangdong range between $286 and $378.

That disparity – worsened by rising inflation and the growing cost of living – pushed the workers to strike and hit the streets on Saturday to demand a minimum wage of 30,000 taka ($241), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($102).

On Sunday, Begum joined one such protest in the Jamgora part of the Ashulia industrial area on the outskirts of the capital Dhaka, with the police firing tear gas and stun grenades to disperse the protesters, and arresting dozens of them.

The ⁠Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association said the demonstrations disrupted operations at 529 factories on Sunday and affected nearly a million workers.

Later that day, the government announced the formation of a six-member wage board to review the workers’ demands.

But that did not stop the garment workers from returning to the streets for a third straight day on Monday.

In northern Dhaka’s Gazipur area, the workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, and vandalised and torched several vehicles, while clashes with police were reported from the neighbouring Mirpur district.

“The government only makes promises,” Begum told Al Jazeera. “They haven’t told us when wages will increase and by how much.”

Rasel Khan, a 30-year-old garment worker at Ashulia, told Al Jazeera his monthly earnings of 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161), including overtime, were no longer enough to support his family, which included his mother and younger brother besides his wife and child.

As living costs soar, he has accumulated a debt of about 100,000 taka ($805) to meet his needs. “It’s impossible to support a family on this income anymore. Prices keep rising, and we have to borrow money just to survive,” he said.

The last revision of the minimum wage in the garment sector took place in December 2023. Since then, prices have continued to climb. Official data put annual inflation at 8.34 percent in September, including 7.22 percent for food and 9.30 percent for non-food expenses.

Begum says she pays 3,500 taka ($28) as rent for a single room shared with her mother and children. Her father, living in their village in the central district of Sirajganj, also depends on her income.

She says she is burning discarded paper and other materials to cook because she is not able to afford a gas cylinder that costs about 2,200 taka ($18).

Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said persistent inflation over the past five years has sharply eroded the purchasing power of low-paid workers.

“When real income falls, they have to cut their daily living standards,” he told Al Jazeera. “They don’t have any surplus income.”

Hussain said a recent hike in the salary of government employees has had a “demonstration effect” among private-sector workers waiting for a similar relief.

The government’s announcement of a wage board follows an amendment to labour laws to reduce the wage review cycle from five years to three years. The current three-year period ends in December.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman convened an emergency meeting of top government officials on Sunday, while Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed met the garment factory owners on Monday, assuring them that a new minimum wage would be fixed through negotiations.

Labour Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury meanwhile urged the workers to resume work, saying the wage board would begin its deliberations shortly.

But Babul Akhter, a workers’ representative on the board, called for the new wages to take effect with January 2027 salaries. He also asked the demonstrators to return to work and demanded the release of arrested workers and withdrawal of cases against them.

The impending wage negotiations come at a challenging time for Bangladesh’s garment industry, as manufacturers balance workers’ demands for better wages with rising production costs and intensifying global competition.

Sheikh Hossain Muhammad Mustafiz, an official at Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association and managing director of Cute Dress Industry Ltd, told Al Jazeera that fair wages and employment security must go hand in hand with their ability to compete in the international market.

“Workers deserve wages that support a decent standard of living. However, without fair purchasing prices from international brands, significant wage increases could put pressure on factories and threaten employment,” he said.
