He denied the accusation that he would pretend to be gay to make women trust him.

Court has adjourned for a break until 2pm.

title: Trump and Vance rally for Republicans in final midterms push; Alaska’s Murkowski backs Democrat in governor’s race – live
excerpt:
Trump heads to Ohio while Vance travels to North Carolina; Republican US senator Lisa Murkowski endorses Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, breaking with her party

Donald Trump will return to Ohio on Wednesday...
body_text:
Trump heads to Ohio while Vance travels to North Carolina; Republican US senator Lisa Murkowski endorses Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, breaking with her party

Donald Trump will return to Ohio on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans in the state, as the GOP looks to hold on to the seat currently occupied by Senator Jon Husted. Husted’s opponent, Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator from the state, has a decent lead in the polls with less than a week remaining until election day.

Up until now, Trump has made a habit of praising Husted’s physique (his butt, especially) on the campaign trail. We’ll see if he keeps that up today.

JD Vance, perhaps Trump’s busiest surrogate on the campaign trial, will continue a cross-country air campaign by heading east to North Carolina, where he’ll back Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is trailing in the polls to Democratic former governor Roy Cooper.

While stumping on behalf of Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Maine, Senator Mark Kelly teased a possible run for president in 2028.

“I’m considering it,” the Democratic lawmaker for Arizona said at a campaign event for Maine veterans in Brunswick. “I’ll make a decision after this election sometime.”

Kelly noted the weight of the decision. “You know, I’ve always served this country … usually in the cockpit, strapped into the rocket ship,” he said. “By far, the most important job I’ve ever had is the one I have now,” he said referring to his role as a first-term US senator.

“If I screw it up in the rocket ship, it just gets blown up. People get over it in a week. This is different. I mean, this is 350 million people, and people around the world. It’s important that the United States maintains its position of leadership in the world,” Kelly added.

For months, Mary Peltola’s campaign for Alaska’s Senate seat has denied any connection to a separate campaign launched by a man who, coincidentally, shares the exact same name as Peltola’s Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan.

New reporting from the New York Times undercuts that claim. The outlet reported, based on interviews, obtained text messages and legal filings, that the Peltola campaign had not only recruited Mr Sullivan (not the Republican), but had sought out a number of Dan Sullivans across the state for potential candidacy, as well as others who could peel votes away from Peltola’s main opponent.

Tactics like those the Times claims Peltola used are not unheard of, and are generally considered legal, if perhaps underhanded, election strategies. Still, the Department of Justice has sued to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if votes cast for the other Dan Sullivan cost the Republican candidate the race.

Since he took office last year, Bill Essayli, southern California’s highest-ranking federal prosecutor, has wielded his office to help advance Trump’s policies, including on immigration and transgender rights.

Now, he’s using that same authority to try and block tens of thousands of California votes from being counted in the upcoming midterm elections. Specifically, Essayli has sued to make the state aside ballots from 20,000 voters who the Department of Justice has branded “likely noncitizens”.

Experts in constitutional law said that it was an extraordinary step for a nominally independent DoJ to seek to disqualify so many ballots in the name of fighting alleged noncitizen voter fraud that, despite Trump’s insistence, has proven vanishingly rare.

My colleague Sam Levin has the story here:

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, faced backlash on Wednesday for a “wildly racist tirade” during a campaign stop in Michigan in which he falsely asserted that Arabs never won major awards in science or literature.

Kennedy was speaking at the Monday night event in Grand Rapids in support of Mike Rogers, the Republican US Senate candidate trailing his Democratic midterms opponent Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, in polling.

“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the ⁠Nobel prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf prize, they don’t produce literature,” Kennedy said.

A factcheck published on Tuesday by the Associated Press showed that Arabs have won, or been shortlisted, for all those awards in recent years.

The ⁠Council on American-Islamic Relations called Kennedy’s Islamophobic remarks “a ⁠textbook display of ​unvarnished racism and bigotry”, and the US healthcare advocacy organization Protect Our Care condemned his “wildly racist tirade”.

Hillary Scholten, a Democratic congresswoman representing west Michigan, who declined to endorse El-Sayed this summer, said Kennedy’s comments were “disgraceful and have no place in public service”.

In a statement posted to her Facebook page late Tuesday, Scholten said: “As secretary of health and human services, he has a responsibility to serve all Americans, not use his position to demean entire communities with bigoted and demonstrably false claims”.”

She added: “The last I checked, Secretary Kennedy has neither a medical degree nor a Nobel peace prize, and his rhetoric has undermined public confidence in health science. Maybe he should sit this one out.”

Other Trump administration officials have tried to paint El-Sayed as a supporter of Islamic radicalism, including the president himself, who at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday called the Democrat “a jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists”.

Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro who recently lost the race for his father’s former office, has landed in Miami, apparently taking shelter under the aegis of the Trump administration after fleeing his home country.

The younger Bolsonaro had been ordered to turn over his passport following his election defeat in connection with a criminal investigation over money laundering. Instead, Reuters and other outlets have reported that the defeated candidate and his family fled to Argentina overland before flying to the US via Ecaudor.

He has so far refused to officially concede the race to the victorious left-wing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Trump has said that Brazilian election appeared “rigged,” but gave little indication he would seek to get involved in disputing the results.

Though Trump did not outright endorse Flavio Bolsonaro, his father Jair was a close ideological ally of Trump’s in Latin America. After Brazil launched a criminal prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro for allegedly attempting a coup to restore him to power after his 2022 election loss, Trump slapped tariffs on the country in retaliation.

And there is little love between Trump and Lula, who has accused Trump of trying to meddle in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favor.

Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, has broken with her party to endorse the Democrat in her state’s gubernatorial contest.

Murkowski, a moderate Republican who is no stranger to breaking with Trump, made her surprise endorsement to local news station KTUU. She told the outlet that she felt the three Republicans contesting Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the ranked-choice election lacked the bipartisanship needed for the job, calling them overly partisan.

She said that Kreiss-Tomkins, by contrast, is “a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now, a freshness of energy”. She described him as a “a commonsense guy who has a known ability to be working together”.

Donald Trump will return to Ohio on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans in the state, as the GOP looks to hold on to the seat currently occupied by Senator Jon Husted. Husted’s opponent, Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator from the state, has a decent lead in the polls with less than a week remaining until election day.

Up until now, Trump has made a habit of praising Husted’s physique (his butt, especially) on the campaign trail. We’ll see if he keeps that up today.

JD Vance, perhaps Trump’s busiest surrogate on the campaign trial, will continue a cross-country air campaign by heading east to North Carolina, where he’ll back Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is trailing in the polls to Democratic former governor Roy Cooper.

Former president Barack Obama will travel to Georgia tonight to campaign alongside top Democrats in the state, including incumbent senator Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta now seeking the Georgia governor’s office.

Obama has been increasingly active on the campaign trail as the midterms race nears its climax. The former president recently joined rallies in Ohio and Michigan, two states where Democrats are looking to win out closely contested Senate races, before setting his sights on Georgia.

During his previous stop in Ohio, Obama made a jab at Trump for redecorating the White House to look like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”. The remark appeared to get under Trump’s skin, prompting him to respond, and has somehow drawn the restaurant chain into the battle for control of Congress.

In Georgia, Ossoff, who is facing a Senate challenge from Republican House representative Mike Collins, holds a comfortable lead in the polls. Increasingly, the Gerogia Democrat has been seen as a potential contender for the Democrats’ nomination in the 2028 presidential election.

The race is much tighter for Bottoms, who is vying to flip Georgia’s governor’s office red.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the rightwing Brazilian presidential candidate who lost the country’s election to leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is expected to arrive in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil, Reuters reported.

According to the outlet, Bolsonaro and his family – after crossing by land into Argentina, and from there departing to Ecuador – took a flight bound for the US, where the Trump administration’s state department plans to grant them visas.

Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-allied former leader of Brazil who was arrested and handed a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn the result of his own 2022 election defeat to Lula. After his election defeat by Lula over the weekend, and before fleeing to the US, he had been ordered to turn over his passports in connection with a criminal investigation.

Trump did not outright endorse the younger Bolsonaro this time around. But he has publicly sparred with Lula frequently in his second term, including imposing tariffs on Brazil in response to its criminal prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. And Trump has boasted about his role as an apparent kingmaker in Latin America, where Brazil is one of the few holdouts still controlled by leftwing governments as rightwing leaders are ascendent through the region.

Throughout his re-election campaign, Lula accused the Trump administration of trying to interfere with the vote, and of having colonial ambitions in Brazil.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last rate-setting meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.

Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.

The move infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.

Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, a pause would signal the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.

Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.

Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.

“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

A federal judge has ruled that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top US prosecutor in Los Angeles.

Essayli was disqualified from overseeing two criminal prosecutions. The order, however, will not immediately go into effect, and the Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it intends to appeal.

The ruling was part of a long-running legal battle challenging the Trump administration’s maneuvers to keep Essayli in office despite not being confirmed by the US Senate.

Essayli, a former Republican state lawmaker and ally of Donald Trump, became an interim US attorney in April 2025, but he was not formally nominated by the president, which allowed him to lead the office without going through the standard confirmation process.

After Essayli’s “interim” appointment ended last July, the Trump administration gave him an “acting” title, then kept him on as a “first assistant” after a judge ruled he was unlawfully serving as US attorney.

But in August, a federal appellate court ruled against a Nevada justice department leader in a similar case, and the judge overseeing Essayli’s case cited that higher court’s ruling on Tuesday, issuing another order saying he was still acting unlawfully.

Michael Seabright, the federal judge, said Essayli was illegally serving, even with a “special attorney” and “first assistant” designation by the Trump administration, and the judge said he could no longer participate in or supervise two ongoing prosecutions where the attorneys had challenged his position.

“We respectfully disagree with the court’s order,” Essayli said in a statement on Tuesday. “The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”

Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which the president said had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.

A senior state department official told the Associated Press that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States”.

In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.

Trump lied that “our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama – our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama”.

title: In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely
excerpt:
A movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next

Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox...
body_text:
A movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next

Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond.

In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after a deadly roof collapse at the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met with baton-wielding police, teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors.

Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the students explained in an open letter to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.”

On Sunday, their movement made headlines across the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power. In a ballot that saw the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992, over 50% of voters backed the students to oust the increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and end his party’s 14 years in power.

It was, as a Guardian editorial noted, “one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.

The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to the common thread that weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.

The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matković noted this week. Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?

Matković drew on his involvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.

Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24, told the Guardian.

Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this time to clean up after a night of raucous celebrations.

The movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s party had transformed the state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.

The movement won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosen via student assemblies in the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday, the top priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movement wrote in the Guardian this week. “Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”

And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The country applied to join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the elections have ushered in the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.

As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.

Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.

It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.

title: Death toll rises to 68 with dozens injured after high-speed train collision in Spain – latest updates
excerpt:
Pedro Sánchez says the government will act with urgency to ‘clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred’

At least 68 people have been killed after two passenger trains collided in Toledro pr...
body_text:
Pedro Sánchez says the government will act with urgency to ‘clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred’

At least 68 people have been killed after two passenger trains collided in Toledro province in central Spain, and the death toll may rise further.

A similar number of people remain hospitalised, including 15 in serious or critical state (15:44).

The two trains with 544 people on board in total (10:46) were travelling in the same direction on the high-speed line from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south-west of the country.

Video footage from the scene showed extensive damage to both trains (12:23, 13:52).

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said the country was “in mourning” as he insisted the government will get to the bottom of incident and address potential failures with “utmost firmness” (15:49).

Transport minister Óscar Puente said initial review of the evidence pointed to an “inexplicable” decision to order trains to go ahead after a signalling failure (15:01), implying a human error.

Spanish media reported that the controller responsible was questioned by investigators this afternoon (16:40).

Today’s collision is the second high-profile train crash in Spain this year (11:00), and the third deadliest incident on its railway in the last 50 years (12:55).

Spain is expected to declare three days of mourning later today (15:54).

Both main parties suspended their campaigning activities ahead of next month’s parliamentary election, but the far-right Vox party continued with its rallies (12:11).

Spain’s Civil Guard is questioning the traffic controller responsible for the stretch of track where the crash happened, according to the Europa Press news agency.

Their inquiries are part of an investigation opened by Spain’s railway accident investigation commission, CIAF, Europa press said.

Earlier today, Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente pointed to an “inexplicable” call to resume traffic at full speed after a signalling failure, implying a potential human error behind the crash (15:01).

In the last few minutes, the opposition People’s party (PP)‘s leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo responded to the incident near Urda.

In a sombre speech, Feijóo expressed his solidarity with all affected and their families, and thanked emergency services for their response.

But he said that “our grief does not compel us to remain silent,” as he said the Spanish people will be “rightfully asking questions – and they deserve answers.”

He called for an immediate government investigation and a judicial inquiry into the crash, “utilising all available resources and free from interference.”

He also demanded a response to growing concerns about the state of infrastructure, as he called for “a comprehensive, independent review of the entire railway network.”

“This can no longer be delayed; the public has a right to full accountability for every euro.”

He also confirmed that his party has for now suspended all campaigning events ahead of next month’s parliamentary election as a sign of respect for the victims and their families (unlike the far-right Vox party).

Sánchez also says he will declare three days of mourning – starting tomorrow, 29 October to 31 October.

“Spain is in mourning and embraces the victims; the government of Spain – and the entire State – stands with the victims and their families.”

He says “Spain is in mourning” as he expresses “solidarity and empathy” with all affected.

He says the government’s first priority is to focus on helping the victims and their families.

He also thanks all emergency services for their work.

He says the government needs to “clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred,” working alongside the independent railways accident investigators and judicial authorities.

“If there has been any negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness,” he says.

Sánchez points out that the two high-profile high-speed train crashes of recent months – this one and in Adamuz in January – seem to have different causes.

But he says the government “must further strengthen safety to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail network.”

“This is essential, as it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to experience two high-speed rail accidents in a single year,” he says.

But first, the Castilla – La Mancha president Emiliano García-Page speaks about his “deep, profound” sorrow over today’s incident.

He says the latest data suggest at least 68 fatalities.

There are also some 15 people with severe or critical injuries, and 53 people who required hospitalisation for moderate injuries.

During his visit to the site of the crash, Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez will be accompanied by interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska and local government president Emiliano García-Page.

We are expecting a press statement at some point.

Astonishingly, Puente suggests there was more than one incorrect order; a similar instruction to resume was also ordered to at least one other train, with the train driver going back to the traffic control to push back on the order.

That ends this press conference, but we will no doubt hear more about the circumstances of the incident later today.

Puente says that while a signalling failure “can happen”, there are strict standard procedures for how to proceed in such cases, as he once again heavily hints at a combination of technical and human errors.

He says the order to restart traffic should not have been issued, and that even if it was taken, the train in question should have been instructed to restart “on sight” – meaning driver should only move very slowly, under strict restrictions, at maximum 40km/h, and not at normal speed.

He says the person responsible for the decision is now under investigation.

He does not answer a question if he intends to resign.

Puente begins by paying tribute to all affected by the crash.

“We are absolutely devastated; as you can well imagine, this is one of the most difficult moments one could ever face,” he says.

He says a rear-end collision is an unusual thing on the Spanish network, which is why his enquiries focused on understanding what happened.

He has he has been able to see a full reconstruction of the incident and review audio recordings of all communications between the affected trains and the traffic control.

He says that around 8:30am this morning, the LZB controlling system failed due to communications issues, leaving no coverage for just over 60km of the track, which in turn triggered an automatic stop for six trains on that stretch.

But around 8:36, the Adif control centre issued a manual instruction to override the warning and let the traffic resume.

He heavily suggests that this “inexplicable” decision should not have been made, as trains should have remained under strict orders not to move.

During the next 25 minutes, the second AVE train travelled 25 kilometers and eventually collided with a stationary Iryo train.

“This is the account of events that I can provide,” he says.

Spanish transport minister Óscar Puente is speaking now, but he’s having some audio issues with his microphone that they are trying to sort out.

Once that’s resolved, I will bring you his key lines here.

UK ambassador to Spain Alex Ellis expressed his concern about the incident and support to all affected.

“If you are a British national and you or a family member have been affected by the train crash and require consular support, call the nearest British Consulate on 0034 91 714 6300.”

We are also getting some first pictures from emergency reception areas supporting those affected by the crash.

title: ‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget
excerpt:
OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

British househ...
body_text:
OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

British households face a “pretty grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said.

In a report as John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances despite the measures taken by the chancellor.

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help households and businesses with soaring energy costs, the watchdog slashed its growth forecasts for 2027 and warned that inflation was poised to reach close to 4% as Britain’s early resilience to the war fizzles out.

While growth this year was upgraded from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, the watchdog slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%.

Highlighting the damage from Donald Trump’s war in the Gulf, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for governments worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule, which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.

As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

The outlook for household disposable income in the UK was “a pretty grim picture”, David Miles of the OBR said.

“If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said. “That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.”

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills.

Despite the measures, the OBR warned that households would come under sustained pressure, with per-person disposable incomes taking account of inflation expected to fall in the short-term before rising modestly before the end of the current parliament.

Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said income levels would only be about 2% above pre-pandemic levels by the start of the 2030s.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

Healey sought to use his budget to harness the power of the technology to boost growth in future while also safeguarding the country against the risk of cyber-attacks amid the accelerating global AI race.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.

“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Donald Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

title: Democrat's 2-word answer on a possible presidential run draws cheers from Maine crowd
excerpt:
While speaking to a crowd of Troy Jackson supporters in Maine, Sen. Mark Kelly appeared to openly express interest in launching a White House bid.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., appeared to leave the door...
body_text:
While speaking to a crowd of Troy Jackson supporters in Maine, Sen. Mark Kelly appeared to openly express interest in launching a White House bid.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., appeared to leave the door open for a presidential run in 2028 while giving a stump speech on Tuesday for Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine.

Kelly was in the middle of an argument about how the economy no longer works for young Americans when an audience member interrupted him with a suggestion about his political future.

"I'm the son of two cops who went to public schools and went on to become a Navy pilot and then an astronaut and now a US senator. I was fortunate," he said.

Just as Kelly mentioned becoming a senator, someone in the crowd shouted "president," prompting a two-word response from the Arizona Democrat.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., speaks during a meet-and-greet event held by Kelly and Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson ahead of the midterm elections in Freeport, Maine, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Reuters/Taylor Coester)

WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’

"We'll see," said Kelly, whose short response drew cheers from the crowd.

Kelly, who is up for re-election in 2028, is routinely featured in 2028 Democratic presidential primary surveys and often polls below more established contenders like former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Still, Kelly has begun gaining support as his national profile rises. He drew widespread attention in Nov. 2025 after appearing in a video alongside other Democratic lawmakers telling U.S. service members that it is their duty to disobey illegal orders, including those issued by the executive branch.

The video prompted a criminal investigation into Kelly and the five other Democratic lawmakers, although a federal grand jury declined to indict them in February.

HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026

Axios reported last week that Kelly is eying a run for the White House. He told the outlet that he will decide whether he is running for president or another term in the Senate after the midterms.

However, Kelly would not necessarily have to choose between the two. Under Arizona law, presidential and vice presidential candidates are permitted to simultaneously seek election to one additional federal office, meaning Kelly could run for both president and Senate in 2028.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., greets a supporter at a campaign event for Senate candidate Troy Jackson in Freeport, Maine on Oct. 27, 2026. (Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images)

The provision in Arizona law could make a presidential bid less of a political gamble for Kelly, allowing him to pursue the highest office in the land without necessarily jeopardizing his Senate career.

If Kelly secures the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, he could appear on Arizona ballots as a candidate for both president and the Senate, though he wouldn't be able to occupy both offices if he won both races.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: What is the controversy between Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe and China?
excerpt: Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe is at the centre of a controversy in China for his comments on late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, which have not only cost him several commercial deals but have also led to st...
body_text:
Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe is at the centre of a controversy in China for his comments on late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, which have not only cost him several commercial deals but have also led to state television scrapping La Liga broadcasts.

The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands ⁠in the lucrative Chinese market, where satire about Mao, modern China’s founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.

Once hailed as a footballing sensation, Mbappe was widely adored in China until the controversy caused outrage among the country’s 1.4 billion people.

Despite issuing an apology, the French superstar struggled to dissipate anger on Chinese social media on Wednesday.

Al Jazeera breaks down the row between Mbappe and China:

A video circulated online showed France’s 2018 World Cup winner Mbappe apparently joking about a former Chinese leader.

While Mbappe did not name Mao in the video, he appeared to say the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face digitally altered onto that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.

The video, which shows Mbappe preparing to go on air, was purportedly filmed in April, as verified by Al Jazeera.

The clip was shared by French football podcast The Bridge and widely circulated on social media on Monday. It has since been taken down.

Fans ‌have previously created memes superimposing Mbappe’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for.

Mbappe, who has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press, said last month that he acknowledged the humour, but did not like being compared with figures associated with tragedies.

“There’s a part of it that’s funny. You can tell that, for some people, it’s all in good fun. But there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said in an interview with French sports newspaper L’Equipe.

The “dictator Mbappe” memes began as caricatures of his influence at Paris Saint-Germain, not statements of political allegiance.

By apparently laughing at an ⁠image depicting him as Mao, however, the France captain entered territory in which self-mockery could be perceived as an insult to a country’s founding leader.

Mbappe’s original joke was not reposted – or had been scrubbed – from China’s tightly controlled social media, with state media omitting any references to Mao, saying instead that the footballer had made “inappropriate remarks concerning China”.

But Mbappe has faced a torrent of criticism from China.

“His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated,” wrote one user on social media platform Weibo.

Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu had meanwhile frozen Mbappe’s account, where he has at least a million followers, preventing him from gaining any new ones.

The same was done on the Weibo app, with a notice stating that “the user has been banned from following due to violating laws or the Weibo Community Convention”.

In China, satire or jokes about Mao are considered disrespectful.

“A remark about an internet meme has triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the ‌‌limits of celebrity influence,” state media outlet China Daily said.

Mbappe – one of the world’s most prominent athletes – has become the latest sports star to fall foul of a faux pas in China.

Many Chinese media outlets condemned Mbappe’s apparent remarks, but did not repeat them.

“What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,” the state-backed Global Times said.

“The message from Chinese consumers is clear: respect is not optional; one doesn’t get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance.”

The French football star was dropped by two major brands in China: Dongpeng and Mengniu.

Chinese drinks giant Dongpeng said on Tuesday it terminated its contract with Mbappe “with immediate effect”.

“Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” it said in a statement.

Advertisements showing AI-generated images of Mbappe drinking a Dongpeng sports drink were regularly shown in China during this year’s World Cup.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, also cut ties with Mbappe, who, until this incident, was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of followers on social media.

Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappe-related content on Weibo.

Offline too, the Mbappe brand appeared to be scrubbed from stores.

The AFP news agency said that when it visited the Adidas flagship store in Beijing’s Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid jerseys were available for sale, but none bearing Mbappe’s name.

Mbappe apologised for his “ill-judged” comment, saying he understood it hurt the Chinese people.

“My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” Mbappe wrote in a statement published on his social media accounts on Tuesday.

The 27-year-old said he “reacted to an image of myself” during the interview.

“I apologise to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.”

The statement was published in French, Mandarin and English.

China said on Wednesday it took “seriously” the apology from Mbappe.

“We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

Yes. China’s state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving La Liga and Mbappe, and all advertisements involving Mbappe have been removed, the state-backed media outlet The Paper reported on Tuesday.

“Mbappe’s team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about,” said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T Burns Sports Group.

Global sporting figures who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors.

China suspended sponsorship deals with the NBA while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.

La Liga President Javier Tebas said that he held a meeting with the ambassador of China in Spain to address the situation and “seek solutions that allow us to overcome this episode”.

“Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions,” Tebas said in a statement posted to social media.

“China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for La Liga.”

Earlier on Tuesday, Tebas issued an apology and said ⁠La Liga deeply regretted the alleged comments that caused discomfort and offence in China.

The Reuters news agency reported on Wednesday that Tebas was considering travelling to China to neutralise the threat of a massive financial loss for ⁠Spanish football.

Tebas and Real share a strained relationship due to a power struggle within Spanish football, but both parties have put aside their differences, acknowledging the potential immediate ⁠and long-term financial repercussions of Mbappe’s comments.

Real Madrid on ⁠Wednesday ⁠issued an apology.

“Real Madrid CF ‌wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort caused by the recent words of our ⁠player Kylian Mbappe,” Real ⁠said in a statement.

“Our club maintains a deep respect for ⁠China, its history, its culture ⁠and its citizens, ⁠as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who ‌feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid,” the statement ‌added.

title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
excerpt:
Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene

Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.

Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe t...
body_text:
Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene

Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.

Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.

So far at least 68 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.

Here is what we know about the crash so far.

The two trains collided just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.

The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country collided with another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.

Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.

Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.

All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.

Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.

A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.

Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown.

Transport minister Oscar Puente has said a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.

"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre which decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.

That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.

Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response

More than 500 people were believed to be on board both trains.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.

A former government minister was also among those reported missing.

The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, Fátima Báñez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.

The Castilla La Mancha regional government said 64 people are now confirmed to have died.

Speaking separately to Spanish media, he warned the death toll could increase further.

Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition, and 15 more in a critical condition.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".

"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.

The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.

"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.

"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

Sánchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.

Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.

A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.

A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.

Hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".

It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.

This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.

In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

title: GSK shares dive as weaker vaccine sales unnerve investors
excerpt:
British pharma company one of biggest fallers on FTSE 100 despite better than expected financial results

Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financ...
body_text:
British pharma company one of biggest fallers on FTSE 100 despite better than expected financial results

Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financial results, as investors were unnerved by weaker sales of its respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and shingles vaccines and recently launched medications.

Britain’s second-biggest pharmaceutical company reported a 19% decline in pre-tax profit to £1.9bn in the July to September quarter and £318m of restructuring charges, with more to come. Core operating profit and core earnings per share rose 5% and 1% respectively, however, beating analysts’ expectations.

Shares dived as much as 7% at one point on Wednesday, and despite later paring back such losses to a 3.8% drop, it was the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index of blue-chip businesses.

Luke Miels, who took over from Emma Walmsley as GSK’s chief executive in January, has announced a number of acquisitions, including a £7.9bn US cancer specialist and a major cost-saving programme in July to speed up drug development.

GSK said turnover in the third quarter was £8.9bn, a 5% rise compared with the same period last year thanks to strong sales of its HIV, cancer and lupus medications.

Vaccine sales, however, dipped 2% to £2.6bn, with sharp declines for the shingles shot Shingrix, down 5%, and the RSV vaccine Arexvy, down 24%, partly the result of tough year-on-year comparisons, while sales of meningitis vaccines rose 12%. Sales of the recently launched asthma drug Exdensur also disappointed analysts.

Referring to Arexvy, Miels said: “When we look at our market share versus Pfizer, we still have leadership there. We are getting good orders outside of the US, so I think we need to just see what happens over the next couple of months to have the full picture.”

Investors are also worried about the loss of patent protection for GSK’s blockbuster HIV drug dolutegravir towards the end of the decade, which means other drugmakers can make cheaper, generic versions.

GSK has set a goal of generating more than £40bn in total annual revenue by 2031 as it rebuilds its cancer business.

Miels said the company was slightly ahead on its three-year cost reduction plan to save £1.9bn a year, which involves simplifying operations to invest more in research and development (R&D). The restructuring will cost the company £2.4bn, and most of these charges will come this year and next.

The impact on the UK was relatively limited, Miels said, with some cuts to support jobs such as in human resources and procurement at its headquarters in central London and in hubs in Poland and India. “You never want headquarters to be too big; I want people on the bench in the lab,” he said.

GSK is also reorganising its vaccine business in Belgium, with increased use of ​digital tools and automation expected to lead to about 1,200 job losses, but the country will continue to produce the bulk of its vaccines. GSK had nearly 67,000 employees globally at the end of last ​year, its annual report showed.

GSK stuck to its annual forecasts, with R&D spending set to grow ​faster than sales. It expects to begin 22 late-stage studies of new medications by the end of the year.

Miels said Shingrix had the “potential to grow next year”, describing it as “a remarkable product”. He pointed to two large studies of the vaccine to assess the reduction of dementia risk, as well as its effects on major adverse cardiovascular events such as heart attacks and strokes, with the first data available in 2029 and 2027 respectively.

Both studies could be “transformative” for the shingles vaccine, he added.

Britain’s high street chemists have reported a rise in demand for the shingles vaccine after studies showed a correlation with a reduced risk of dementia. “We’ve got a lot of studies that show a correlation. We’re trying to demonstrate causation,” Miels said.

title: Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs
excerpt:
The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices

A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was...
body_text:
The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices

A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices.

The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press. The ship has a 650-passenger capacity.

The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”.

“Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives over the next 60 days.”

The ship is now docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with a departure date still unclear.

The price of fuel across the world has jumped since the start of the US war on Iran earlier this year. The ship’s operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800.

The strait of Hormuz, which transports much of the world’s oil, has effectively been closed since 28 February, the beginning of the war. Oil prices climbed to above $117 a barrel this month.

One resident on the ship, Randy Cassingham, wrote in a blogpost that he only discovered the cruise route’s cancellation after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship on Monday morning.

“It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote. “It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.”

Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health.

Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. Despite the issues, however, Larson said she did not regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” she said. “From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising.”

title: Rays ride walk-off momentum into Game 5 after stunning 12th-inning comeback in World Series
excerpt:
Brewers manager Pat Murphy discusses Milwaukee's dramatic extra-inning Game 4 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays and preparing for Game 5.

For a series that is lopsided in terms of the outcomes, this ha...
body_text:
Brewers manager Pat Murphy discusses Milwaukee's dramatic extra-inning Game 4 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays and preparing for Game 5.

For a series that is lopsided in terms of the outcomes, this has actually been a really entertaining World Series. It doesn't matter that one team is up 3-1 in the Fall Classic; the games have been exciting. Well, all of them except Game 3. The Brewers are set up to win tonight with their best pitcher on the mound, and the Rays are hopeful that yesterday's win leads to another one today.

The Milwaukee Brewers had all sorts of emotions yesterday. They once again came back in a game and took a lead. That's been the case for the Brewers in most games this postseason. It seems like the other team scores, the Brewers respond with a bigger punch, and then they turn to a bullpen that has been elite all postseason. It is hard to believe that Milwaukee has been this consistently good in the playoffs, but they finally stumbled a bit last night.

RAYS' COMEBACK EXTRA-INNINGS VICTORY IN WORLD SERIES GAME 4 GIVES TEAM KERNEL OF HOPE, HISTORY SHOWS

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski (33) throws a pitch during the third inning against the St. Louis Cardinals at American Family Field. (Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images)

Tonight, they have the upper hand by sending the best pitcher in baseball this year to close out the World Series. Jacob Misiorowski takes the ball tonight. In the regular season, he was 16-5 and led the Majors in ERA, strikeouts, and WHIP. He hasn't quite been unhittable in the playoffs, but he's been very good. Additionally, his arm really shouldn't be tired, as this is the first time anyone has had the opportunity to face him a second time. In 13.1 innings this postseason, he has allowed four earned runs on 13 hits and five walks. He still has 14 strikeouts as well, but this is still a lot to ask of a 24-year-old.

The Tampa Bay Rays have to feel thrilled to get the monkey off their back last night. After dropping the first three games of the series, the Rays had their backs against the wall, and they were down to their final three outs. In the 12th inning, they found a way to make it work. After giving up a homer in the top half of the inning, they led off with a sharp hit ball to third. Junior Caminero lumbered down the first-base line, and thanks to a throwing error, the Rays had a runner on first to start the inning.

BRONX, NY - JULY 29: Tampa Bay Rays Third Baseman Junior Caminero (13) prior to a Major League Baseball game between the Tampa Bay Rays and the New York Yankees on July 29, 2025, at Yankee Stadium in The Bronx, NY. (Photo by Gregory Fisher/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Gregory Fisher/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

It was a bit strange that Caminero, clearly injured, wasn't pulled from the game. The next hitter, Liam Hicks, hit a ball that found a hole, and Caminero made it to third. Then DeLuca singled to center and tied the game. Chandler Simpson hit another single, but it wasn't deep enough to score a run.

After the Rays sent a pinch hitter to the plate, he chopped a ball over Jake Bauers' head, and the Rays walked off the field happy. What was most impressive for them is that they got four hits in the inning and had only five hits in the first 11 frames.

Tampa Bay Rays' Junior Caminero celebrates a two-run home run against the Cleveland Guardians during the seventh inning in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series in St. Petersburg, Fla., on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/David J. Phillip)

Momentum is a funny thing. The Brewers had all of the momentum in the top of the 12th after a Cooper Pratt homer. Then the Rays took it back. Did they take it for the series, though? I think they might've. Look, facing Misiorowski is not going to be fun or easy, but I think the Rays might have a bit of confidence finally. Maybe it was just a blip in the Brewers' championship run, but I am taking the Rays tonight to get another win before the Brewers close it out at home.
