The prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee, which said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.

Turnout among Israeli army personnel was 79.9%, an increase of 6.2% from the 2022 elections, according to the IDF.

In its statement, the IDF said that 809 polling stations were deployed throughout the country’s bases and in combat zones.

Under Israeli electoral law each voter is assigned to a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at; among those afforded this exception are IDF personnel.

Ballot boxes from these special polling stations are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted.

One apparent loser from Tuesday’s election was far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was expected to better his party’s result of six seats from the 2022 elections.

But instead there was stunned silence at the watch party for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) in central Israel as results from the exit polls flashed across the screen, with most channels suggesting the party would remain on just six seats.

Speaking earlier in the evening, Ben-Gvir attempted to revive his supporters spirits by reminding them of all he had achieved in the past four years to further their agenda, including passing a law approving the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of murdering Israelis and worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners.

He also denounced other members of Netanyahu’s coalition who had suggested a unity government with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, which the audience booed loudly.

double quotation markThis is precisely the scenario we warned against – it is a terrible mistake.”

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.

In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.

The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, currently projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.

Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).

They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir in this election”.

However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.

Negotiations with the Joint List, with 10 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinians Israeli citizens, who are currently exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.

With 50% of the vote counted, Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 56 seats under the current vote share.

The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 49 seats and the Palestinian parties on 15 seats.

Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset, and the final seat projection will probably be updated as more votes are counted.

Exits polls earlier in the evening had both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s bloc tied on about 51 seats.

The lead that exit polls gave to the opposition bloc early in the night has disappeared, with Netanyahu’s grouping now neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot.

Israeli television networks gave the two blocs approximately 51 seats each in the 120 member Knesset – well below the 61 needed to govern. Palestinian parties meanwhile saw a surge in support, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.

No single party has ever reached the requisite 61 seats needed to form a government in the Knesset, so parties must work together to form governing coalitions.

President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats – but with the exit polls showing both parties falling short of a majority that process could take weeks.

​Coalition building in Israel has always been difficult because mainstream parties usually refuse to collaborate with parties run by Palestinian citizens​ of Israel. However some have suggested Eisenkot could begin discussions with the Palestinian groupings who have seen a surge in support.

Palestinian grouping Ra’am is seen as a potential kingmaker if Netanyahu fails to secure enough votes to try to form a government. Their leader, Mansour Abbas, participated in a right-leaning government in the past.

However Eisenkot’s camp kept them at arm’s length during the campaign, perceiving their support as a liability. In the past he has said Arab-led parties do not meet Zionist criteria to govern.

For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats, save for defections. Addressing his supporters in the early hours of Wednesday morning, he said that a government that relies on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Coalition negotiations can be arduous and can produce unstable governments. It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.

If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.

In this scenario, lawmakers from the Palestinian parties whose representation in the Knesset is likely to have increase, could play a critical role.

The Joint List – which represents a number of Israeli Arab parties – has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.

While appearing fanciful at first glance, Israeli commentators have mused in recent weeks on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.

Amit Segal, the chief political analyst for Channel 12 and journalist seen as close to Netanyahu, suggested that the prime minister’s extortion that the “Zionist majority must come to its senses and unite”, could be interpreted as an olive branch to Eisenkot.

This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement, but their partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.

A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.

If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.

The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.

However if we a new set of polls is on the horizon, they are not likely to happen for weeks at the minimum, with the candidate designated by the president having 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two week extension.

Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.

The polls published by Israel’s major TV networks show Netanyahu’s governing bloc tied with the opposition grouping led by Eisenkot on 51 seats each, short of the 61 seats needed to form a majority coalition government.

Speaking at 3 am local time, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister vowed to assemble a coalition through agreements between his Likud party, far-right factions and Jewish religious parties.

“We must put in place a strong government of the right,” Netanyahu told cheering supporters. “The Jewish and Zionist majority must unite,” he added.

Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, said earlier in the evening that “people decided in favour of change” and Netanyahu should have “announced today his retirement from politics”.

The election was marked by a record participation by Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin, a discriminated minority that makes up about 20% of the country’s population. Many in the group have sought a stronger political voice after decades of boycotting polls in the Jewish state. Millions of other Palestinians living under Israeli rule in the occupied West Bank and Gaza cannot vote, leading to accusations of apartheid.

Exit polls predicted Palestinian parties could win about 18 seats, up from 10. However, their role in any coalition would be difficult. Netanyahu has said it was “out of the question” to have a government backed by Palestinian parties, while Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties do not meet Zionist criteria to govern.

Donald Trump has said he is “hearing that [Netanyahu] did very well,” speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. “I actually heard he did pretty well.”

Trump cautioned that it was a “little bit early” and said he has not yet spoken with Netanyahu about the results. Trump endorsed Netanyahu late in the campaign, while Netanyahu stressed his close ties with the White House in his election night speech.

Later on, Trump posted a quote to social media, crediting the support he gave to Benjamin Netanyahu for effecting the outcome of the elections, which remain far from clear.

Attributing the lines to “Irving C. Schwartz”, the US president has posted:

double quotation markWhen President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu. It all took place AFTER the Endorsement by President Trump, who only wants what is good for the Middle East, Israel, and the United States of America!”

However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.

Supporters of the opposition bloc breathed a sigh of relief after the first exit polls were announced, but as the night has worn on nervousness has grown on both sides.

With exit polls shifting to put the two sides on equal footing, Agence France-Presse is reporting that voters like former Hamas hostage Ohad Ben Ami have expressed alarm that Netanyahu could come out ahead.

“Three years ago, the government abandoned us,” he said.

double quotation markAn Israeli citizen should never have spent a year and a half in Hamas tunnels when deals [with Hamas] were on the table.”

Netanyahu kept supporters waiting until past 3am in a Jerusalem convention centre. Known for his long, passionate speeches, he was unusually brief.

Ari Marx, holding a large sign bearing the prime minister’s image, said he was not “scared” of the results or of another war with Iran, which Netanyahu has threatened.

“Either Bibi is going to win or there’s going to be a new election,” he said, using Netanyahu’s nickname, doubting anyone else could form a government.

It is also possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.

title: Former world No 3 Stan Wawrinka ends career in home match defeat in Basel
excerpt:
Stan Wawrinka bid farewell to tennis as he brought the curtain down on a decorated 24-year career following a first-round exit at the Basel Open on Tuesday.

The 41-year-old Swiss announced earlier in...
body_text:
Stan Wawrinka bid farewell to tennis as he brought the curtain down on a decorated 24-year career following a first-round exit at the Basel Open on Tuesday.

The 41-year-old Swiss announced earlier in the season that his last tournament as a professional would be the ATP 500-level event in his home country, and a 7-5, 7-6 (7/2) defeat by Czech Jiri Lehecka brought an end to the career of the three-time major champion.

Former world number three Wawrinka, along with Andy Murray, was the only player to win multiple Grand Slams in a period dominated by Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic.

“I was lucky enough to be able to play alongside them and sometimes beat them,” Wawrinka told the AFP news agency in 2024.

He bested Nadal to win his first Grand Slam at the Australian Open in 2014, before beating Djokovic in the French Open final the following season and then again in the US Open title match in 2016.

Alongside his compatriot Federer, the Lausanne native won the Davis Cup for Switzerland and claimed gold in the doubles at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

On court in Basel, Wawrinka’s every point won, as well as several trademark booming one-handed backhands, was greeted by wild cheers from the partisan home crowd.

But Lehecka got his nose in front with a break of serve in the 11th game and sealed the opening set with an ace.

A tight second set went to a tie-break, but it was just a step too far for Wawrinka as his 21st-ranked opponent took firm control to seal the breaker and the match.

Wawrinka, who enjoyed a farewell ceremony in Basel on Monday, did a lap of the court to thank the crowd before disappearing down the tunnel for the last time.

“He won the biggest tournaments, so for me to be here in his moment is a little bit weird,” Lehecka told Sky Sports.

“But at the same time, it’s a pleasure and I will never forget this match.”

However, fans will have one more chance to see the Swiss in action this year.

Wawrinka announced in June that he will throw a farewell party on December 19 in Geneva, with Federer and Murray also on the card for the “One last backhand” event.

Elsewhere, second seed Arthur Fils beat his fellow Frenchman Giovanni Mpetshi Perricard 7-6 (7/5), 7-5 to reach the round of 16.

Spanish third seed Rafael Jodar cruised past Chilean Alejandro Tabilo in straight sets, while top seed Ben Shelton battled past his American compatriot Aleksandar Kovacevic 6-7 (4/7), 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/4).

Djokovic, who trained with his old friend and foe Wawrinka before the tournament on Sunday, will open his campaign on Wednesday against Ugo Humbert of France.

title: Xhaka, Embolo return to Swiss squad after fake COVID docs affair
excerpt: Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka and striker Breel Embolo are available for selection again for next month’s Nations League matches after being sanctioned for using forged COVID-19 certificates during...
body_text:
Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka and striker Breel Embolo are available for selection again for next month’s Nations League matches after being sanctioned for using forged COVID-19 certificates during the pandemic, the Swiss Football Association said.

The pair were dropped and missed the first four Nations League games, in September and October.

Sunderland midfielder Xhaka, 34, who holds a Swiss record 152 caps, admitted to using a forged vaccine certificate to avoid mandatory jabs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Atlanta United forward Embolo, 29, similarly acknowledged that a penal order against him concerned fake COVID certificates.

“The Swiss Football Association (SFV) will once again consider Granit Xhaka and Breel Embolo for the national team, beginning with the Nations League matches in November,” it said in a statement on Tuesday.

“The SFV has thoroughly examined both cases and has concluded that the players’ return is justifiable given the completion of legal proceedings and the sporting consequences incurred [having missed four international matches].”

National team director Pierluigi Tami said: “We are convinced that a return to the national team in November is both responsible and the right course of action.”

Switzerland coach Murat Yakin, his staff and the players’ council unanimously decided that Xhaka will remain the captain.

Switzerland are top of Group B1 in the Nations League, with four straight wins so far.

Yakin will announce his squad for the final two Nations League group matches on November 5. Xhaka and Embolo are on the shortlist, the Swiss FA said.

Switzerland travel to face second-placed Slovenia on November 13, then host Scotland in St Gallen three days later.

“I’m pleased that I can once again make unrestricted selections for the squad in November,” said Yakin.

When the Swiss squad got together in late September, the Lucerne public prosecutor’s office opened an investigation into Xhaka, who admitted obtaining a fake certificate and stepped down.

A few days later, Embolo withdrew from the squad for similar reasons.

Both Xhaka and Embolo were given a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs ($181,225), which will be in place for a probationary period of two years.

The SFV has announced guidelines for handling future matters that involve criminal law.

title: Politics live: ABC calls for One Nation to ‘immediately remove’ Bluey cartoon; RBA says no recession on way
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The ABC has doubled down on its call in Senate estimates for depictions of Bluey to be removed from a One Nation cartoon in which the belov...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The ABC has doubled down on its call in Senate estimates for depictions of Bluey to be removed from a One Nation cartoon in which the beloved character repeatedly runs over politicians with an SUV.

The broadcaster’s managing director, Hugh Marks, said on Tuesday that he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property rights last week and sought legal advice.

double quotation markAs the managing director stated during Senate estimates, the ABC does not own the intellectual property for Bluey.

The ABC is considering available options.

In the meantime, the ABC considers the relevant cartoons should be immediately removed from One Nation’s platforms and no further use should occur.

Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo have been in discussions with the ABC about the issue.

Earlier today, the communications minister, Anika Wells, said the ABC is “well within its rights to be concerned” about One Nation’s use of Bluey, “one of Australia’s biggest, most loved, most well-known exports”.

Labor is main target, not One Nation, David Shoebridge says

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, says Labor is its main target as it looks to double its vote between now and the next federal election to “replace” the governing party.

Following his speech at the National Press Club, Shoebridge was asked what he’s going to do differently given the the party’s vote hasn’t risen much further since the last federal election.

double quotation markThey [Labor] have sold their conscience, and we need to be loud and proud that our job in politics is to do what we said today: to replace the Labor Party.

Yes, we want to fight One Nation, and we want to fight the racism, and division. But they rose on Labor’s watch, and our way to defeat that hate and division is through the Labor Party.

Man charged after allegedly threatening politician on social media

A man has been charged after allegedly using social media to threaten a federal parliamentarian.

The Australian Federal Police arrested the 39-year-old in Lithgow on Tuesday and charged him with using a carriage service to menace, harass or cause offence.

Officers executed a search warrant and allegedly discovered 1 gram of a white crystalline substance and drug paraphernalia, and seized a mobile phone.

The man has also been charged with one count of drug possession and another count of possession of equipment for administration of a prohibited drug.

Opposition questions government on aged care tool consultation process

The shadow aged care minister, Anne Ruston, is asking department officials about there were any meaningful public consultations about the government’s new “escalation pathway” for the aged care assessment tool.

After it was revealed that aged care assessors said the algorithm-driven tool was underquoting on needs of older Australians and assessors had no power to override wrong decisions, the government added a new review pathway.

It means decisions can be escalated to a delegate for review. Aged care assessors have told Guardian Australia this creates more administrative load – they want the ability to override wrong decisions themselves.

Recommendation 4 of the commonwealth ombudsman’s report into the failures of the assessment tool says any changes to aged care legislation should be preceded by open, public consultation.

Ruston asks whether a series of closed-door, targeted workshops met that standard – department officials say consultation was folded into workshops alongside a rapid review with aged care advocacy groups, geriatricians and assessment groups.

Departmental officials say that no draft rules for the pathway were provided to those stakeholders, and no public consultation was conducted. Draft versions of the rules were shared with stakeholders through the minister’s office.

Advocates accuse government of ‘cherrypicking’ welfare compensation recipients

Welfare advocates have accused the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) of “cherrypicking” who might get compensation for having their payment unlawfully cancelled, after it was revealed the department had invited 50,652 to apply, when an estimated 310,000 people were impacted.

The Antipoverty Centre spokesperson and member of the DEWR Targeted Compliance Stakeholder Reference Group Kristin O’Connell said:

double quotation markAll members of the reference group have repeatedly raised our concerns about this process with DEWR and urged them to ensure everyone subjected to these unlawful decisions receives compensation. It is not up to the department to decide whether or not these 300,000 people were harmed – if they made an unlawful decision, they should repay people as an act of good faith.

If people have not been approached but believe they were impacted, they can still apply, with more details here.

The ABC has doubled down on its call in Senate estimates for depictions of Bluey to be removed from a One Nation cartoon in which the beloved character repeatedly runs over politicians with an SUV.

The broadcaster’s managing director, Hugh Marks, said on Tuesday that he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property rights last week and sought legal advice.

double quotation markAs the managing director stated during Senate estimates, the ABC does not own the intellectual property for Bluey.

The ABC is considering available options.

In the meantime, the ABC considers the relevant cartoons should be immediately removed from One Nation’s platforms and no further use should occur.

Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo have been in discussions with the ABC about the issue.

Earlier today, the communications minister, Anika Wells, said the ABC is “well within its rights to be concerned” about One Nation’s use of Bluey, “one of Australia’s biggest, most loved, most well-known exports”.

Jim Chalmers blames Middle East conflict for high inflation

Jim Chalmers has blamed higher global oil prices for intensifying cost of living pressures at home, after inflation jumped to 4.3% in the year to September.

The treasurer in a statement said inflation was “too high”, but that prices were rising faster across a range of countries, not just here.

Fuel prices were up more than 9% last month, and were 24% higher than a year earlier, he said.

double quotation markWe’ve seen higher oil prices driving higher inflation around the world and today’s figures confirm we are not immune from that. From an economic point of view, the [Middle East] conflict can’t end soon enough.

We know this doesn’t make it any easier for families who are under pressure.

The treasurer’s comments come after a sometimes heated debate earlier in the day between the Treasury secretary, Jenny Wilkinson, and Liberal senator Jane Hume around the extent to which government spending was to blame for high inflation.

Sarah Hunter, the RBA’s chief economist, says none of the bank’s real-time economic indicators “are suggesting that the economy is in, or heading into, a recession”.

Speaking at Senate estimates, Hunter’s assessment followed comments by her boss, Michele Bullock, that the Reserve Bank expects unemployment to “gradually move up”, but that “we’re not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage”.

The key jobless measure has climbed to 4.7%, its highest in five years. But it’s still below the 5%-plus pre-Covid level, and the RBA officials’ comments confirm the central bank’s primary worry is high inflation rather than weak growth.

Woolworths CEO says she expects to see ‘modest inflation’ in grocery prices

The Woolworths group chief executive officer, Amanda Bardwell, says she expects “modest inflation” in grocery prices in the near future.

Speaking to journalists after the company released its results for the first quarter of the 2026-2027 financial year, Bardwell said:

double quotation markOverall, what we’d expect as we go forward is to see some modest inflation in food, similar to what we will have seen in previous years.

There’s no doubt that as fuel continues stay at elevated levels and input costs continue to rise, that will cause some suppliers to need to ask for price increases.

Bardwell said there had been a surge in requests from the supermarket’s product suppliers to raise prices earlier in the year, immediately after the war on Iran began, but this reduced “fairly quickly” to a “normalised” number of requests.

Inflation in the food and non-alcoholic beverage sector rose again last month according to the latest official data released this morning by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

The ABS’s consumer price index showed annual inflation in the sector was 3.2% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3% in August 2026.

Aged care algorithm leading to unfair outcomes for older Australians seeking at-home care, estimates hears

More from health estimates: Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne has challenged health and ageing officials at estimates over the aged care algorithm.

Referring to expert testimony and report findings, she argued it pushes critical health issues for older Australians such as dementia, frailty and medication management so far down the decision tree that they barely impact a person’s funding package.
 
 
 The commonwealth ombudsman’s report examined the integrated assessment tool and found it is leading to unreasonable and unfair outcomes for older Australians when it assesses what level of home support older Australians need.

Allman-Payne questioned why complex cognitive and personal health needs are treated as secondary factors by the algorithm.

double quotation markWe’ve heard from functional assessment experts that these are critical domains, and yet, in the way the algorithm is designed … they come in so late in the decision-making tree that at best they move people up one or two levels.
   
   Functional assessment experts are saying … they should be at the front of the algorithm, so that the questions people are being asked at the start.

Department deputy secretary Sonja Stewart pointed to the government’s recently announced independent review into the classification and prioritisation algorithms.

double quotation markThe government will consider and finalise terms of reference for the review that it has announced, in terms of the classification algorithm and the priority algorithm, and the points that you go to are particularly relevant to the classification algorithm and the involvement of experts in that review.

Inflation is ‘too high’, says RBA deputy governor

Andrew Hauser, the RBA’s deputy governor, said this morning’s inflation numbers were “too high”, but also “broadly in line” with what central bank officials and private sector economists were expecting.

Reserve Bank officials are appearing at Senate estimates this morning, and Hauser said the “nightmare” was that longer-term inflation expectations pick up, which would make it harder to get inflation out of the system.

double quotation markWe don’t think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk.

The consumer price index shows that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time as unemployment lifts, making life uncomfortable for many households.

Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.

Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs are up 5.2%.

These are all big components of a typical household budget and are largely unavoidable.

The dynamic feeds into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent over reigniting cost-of-living pressures.

Continuing from the previous post, Rothville was also asked about her husband driving off without paying for petrol last week. What was her reaction?

double quotation markOh look, it was you know the emoji with the hand on the forehead moment. But look, it happens.

She says she was “just upset” she didn’t return her daughter’s friend’s pencil case herself.

Ben Carroll’s wife joins him on campaign trail

Ben Carroll has a special guest on the campaign bus with him today – his wife, Fiona Rothville. He told reporters he’s lucky she’ll be joining him during the campaign as she’s a “great moral support”.

double quotation markI’m very happy to be involved in the campaign. Not every day … It’ll be you know a couple of times of the campaign here and there again, just to support Ben and support my family and balance my responsibilities.

But her appearance comes amid tension at 1 Treasury Place over her involvement in the running of his office. The Herald Sun at the weekend reported Rothville attended briefings and guided policy.

double quotation markWe’re a family that discusses the news, and so you know it’s the standard conversations.

Reporter: “But is he getting your advice on policy?

Rothville: “No. I mean, I’ll have a view on certain things, and we’ll have a chat just like anybody does. “

RBA governor says more pain needed to bring inflation under control

Michele Bullock, the Reserve Bank governor, says “a further period of subdued growth” is needed to bring inflation back under control, ahead of next Tuesday’s decision on whether to deliver a fifth interest rate hike for the year.

Just minutes before the release of the latest inflation figures, Bullock in her opening statement to Senate estimates pointed to a re-escalating Middle East conflict and its impact on fuel prices. She said the AI investment boom was also playing a part in renewed cost-of-living pressures.

double quotation markImportantly though, it is not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia.

While they are certainly compounding the inflation problem, we still see inflation arising from domestic capacity pressures.

The labour market might be “a little bit tighter” than thought despite rising unemployment, and weak productivity is a “fundamental challenge” for the Australian economy, she said.

double quotation markAgainst this backdrop, and despite growth in domestic demand slowing, a further period of subdued growth of aggregate demand is needed to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation down sustainably.

Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.

The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred gauge of consumer prices that strips out volatile items, called underlying inflation, was also elevated at an annual 3.6% to the end of September.

The consumer price index release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another increase to borrowing rates.

The cash rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages, already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four increases this year.

Pauline Hanson decries ‘hypocrites’ in push for early access to super

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has held a press conference as part of the party’s push to allow Australians early access to super to pay rent or make mortgage payments

double quotation markPeople are struggling to keep roofs over their heads. Have we got an obligation for people in this nation to do what we can to assist them now. It is their money.

I’ll raise another point what a bunch of hypocrites – [treasurer Jim] Chalmers and his staff – when members of parliament can access 3% of their super.

But the Super Members Council has estimated a typical 30-year-old worker on that income would end up $25,000 poorer by retirement if they opted in to the One Nation plan.

Poorer retirees would force the government to spend more on the age pension. The SMC estimated the Covid-era withdrawals, where 3 million Australians took out nearly $38bn, would cost taxpayers up to $85bn by the end of the century.

title: Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years in prison in sex trafficking case
excerpt:
Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon, listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf in New York

Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate mog...
body_text:
Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon, listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf in New York

Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate moguls - were sentenced to 30 years each in prison for drugging and raping dozens of women over decades.

Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, were found guilty in March of using their wealth and social status to lure women to parties and luxury homes, where they sexually assaulted them.

"Your conduct was monstrous," said Judge Valerie Caproni before sentencing them. "Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives."

On Tuesday morning, the court in New York heard from 12 victims, including one who did not testify during the trial.

One by one, they spoke of the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them, and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.

Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.

Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety. "I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.

Another victim, using the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16, she lost the ability to trust herself.

"I had no idea the danger I was in till it was too late," she said.

Another woman said when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened her, saying he knew where her sister worked.

Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying facts "paint a truly devastating picture".

"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."

During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they advised their clients not to look at the victims so it couldn't be misconstrued.

Attorneys for the brothers pushed for sentences of 15 years, arguing that they had become devoted fathers whose families would suffer in their absence.

The three men all addressed the court, continuing to profess their innocence.

"We had a work-hard, play-hard mentality," Tal Alexander said, adding he saw how his behavior "hurt people's feelings".

But their statements did not assuage Caproni, who chastised them for refusing to admit their crimes.

"How can someone who never acknowledged the wrongs they did be rehabilitated?" she asked.

At the end of the hearing, she sentenced them each to 30 years in prison for certain crimes. She also sentenced each to 20 years in prison for additional crimes, but said the men would serve the sentences concurrently.

Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa addresses the court and argues for a life sentence during the sentencing of real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon

During the five-week trial, 11 women - several said they were minors at the time of the assaults - testified that the brothers gave them gifts and flew them places including Aspen and the Bahamas where they fed them drugs before raping them.

Prosecutors said the brothers' pattern of abusive behaviour began in high school, though the trial involved crimes starting in 2008.

They said the three slipped drugs into women's drinks, and "physically restrained and held down their victims during the rapes and sexual assaults and ignored screams and explicit requests to stop".

Lawyers for the brothers argued the sex was consensual and that they were womanisers, but not abusers.

Two of the brothers, Tal and Oren, became wealthy selling luxury properties in New York and Miami.

They worked for American real estate giant Douglas Elliman, with clients including Lindsay Lohan, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. In 2022, they founded their own New York-based firm called Official. Alon worked at the family's private security firm, Kent Security.

As they heard their sentences, the brothers stared straight ahead.

title: Australia’s inflation rate rises to 4.3%, fuelling fears of fifth interest rate hike this year
excerpt:
CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our daily...
body_text:
CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.

The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September.

RBA officials have strongly indicated the board may need to lift borrowing costs further to drag price growth back toward its 2.5% target, citing concerns of a “materially worse” inflation outlook.

The CPI release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another cash rate increase.

The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, described the inflation numbers as “too high” at Senate estimates on Wednesday, shortly after the data was released.

He said there was a “nightmare” risk that longer-term inflation expectations would pick up, making it harder to get inflation out of the system.

“We don’t think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk,” Hauser said.

The cash rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages, already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four rate hikes in 2026.

A fierce political debate has erupted in Australia over what is driving the cost-of-living squeeze, with critics pointing to a mix of high fuel prices caused by the Iran conflict, government spending and poor productivity.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said on Wednesday that while “we accept our part in the fight against inflation”, high oil prices and a recovering private sector were the main causes of the rise.

“The most important thing that can happen for Australians under pressure is to see an end to this war in the Middle East,” Chalmers said.

“This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living and for inflation, right around the world.”

CPI figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday show that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time as unemployment lifts, making life uncomfortable for households.

Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.

While higher fuel prices are trickling through the economy, there are price pressures everywhere.

Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%.

Stephen Smith, partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the RBA had “little appetite to allow inflation expectations to drift higher after such a prolonged period above target”.

“The difficulty is that the economy is already slowing. Household spending is subdued, the labour market has softened and the housing market has weakened,” Smith, who is expecting a rate rise next week, said.

The escalating expenses have fed into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent with cost-of-living pressures.

Housing, which is the single biggest category in the CPI, was the largest contributor to annual inflation, according to the ABS, followed by transport costs.

Builders have been passing on higher costs for materials and labour for new dwellings, while electricity prices are also elevated.

Josh Gilbert, market analyst at eToro, said inflation was turning into a “higher-for-longer” story in Australia.

“Anyone holding out for rate relief may need to pack plenty of patience, because another hike looks imminent after today,” Gilbert said.

title: Kylian Mbappé's embarrassing, groveling apology to China comes down to money: Dan Dakich
excerpt: "If you're going to get in bed with Communist China, if you're going to get in bed with somebody that isn't as open and free thinking as we are and Europeans are, then you better shut your damn mouth....
body_text:
"If you're going to get in bed with Communist China, if you're going to get in bed with somebody that isn't as open and free thinking as we are and Europeans are, then you better shut your damn mouth."

It hasn't been the best few months for Kylian Mbappé.

The French superstar striker entered the 2026 World Cup with his team as clear favorites to win the tournament, only to come up well short, losing 2-0 to Spain in the semifinals. Then, on Monday night, he lost the Ballon d'Or, the award given out to the best player in international soccer, to Harry Kane.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Though Mbappé was brilliant in the "El Classico" against Barcelona, scoring a brace in the rivalry match, through the first 10 matches of the La Liga season, Real Madrid's goal differential of +15 pales in comparison to Barca's +29. He also refused to fully wear a shirt worn by the rest of his teammates, to reaffirm Cueta's status as a part of Spain after an unprecedented surge of illegal immigration from Morocco.

KYLIAN MBAPPE PREDICTABLY BENDS THE KNEE AFTER LOSING CHINESE SPONSORS FOR LAUGHING AT MEME OF DICTATOR MAO

France's Kylian Mbappé looks dejected after the match as France are eliminated from the World Cup in Arlington, Texas. (Jerome Miron/Imagn Images)

But on Tuesday, his season somehow got even worse.

Mbappé bent the knee to China and the Chinese Communist Party, after an appearance on "The Bridge," a French talk show hosted by a teammate, Aurelien Tchouameni. His big offense? Laughing at a meme.

The one "that makes me laugh the most," he said, is "the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator, they put my [face over it]. The show then cut to an example of the meme, his face covering an image of what looks to be Mao Zedong.

Mao was, by any reasonable definition, a dictator. And a brutal, malicious, and violent one. Most historians blame Mao's policies for tens of millions of deaths through famine and politically motivated persecution. It's not a stretch to describe him as evil, and one of history's greatest villains.

But in the modern world of professional sports, there are a few protected groups that must be protected at all costs, and the Chinese Communist Party is one of them. Why? Because there's money to be made for La Liga and Real Madrid in China, and telling the truth about the CCP's abuses is apparently forbidden.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé wrote in a humiliating statement on Tuesday. "I apologize to everyone my words have upset. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid reacts to a missed chance during the LaLiga match between Real Madrid CF and Real Sociedad at Estadio Santiago Bernabeu on May 25, 2025 in Madrid, Spain. (Diego Souto/Getty Images)

If that wasn't enough, the entire Spanish soccer league added their own groveling, ridiculous apology.

"La Liga deeply regrets the offense caused by Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. To the extent of our institutional responsibility, we apologize on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs," the league said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

He's just the latest in a long list of athletes and personalities whose concern for human rights and social justice ends at the Chinese border. And OutKick's Dan Dakich took him to task for how he handled it.

"I don't think people fully understand soccer is, and how big soccer players like Mbappé are, all across the world. Mbappé, if you remember, one of the stars of the World Cup when he came to the USA," Dakich said.

"Mbappé has all kinds of commercials, all kinds of billboards, all kinds of business interests all over China, including anything from cheese to soft drinks ... you name it, he's got a huge, huge presence in China. Well, that's all being threatened to go away, because as you know based on what happened with Daryl Morey and others, China doesn't take kindly to any kind of slur."

Bottles of Dongpeng Beverage Group's "Bushuila" electrolyte drink featuring French football star Kylian Mbappe on the packaging are displayed at a convenience store in Beijing on October 27, 2026. Kylian Mbappe was dropped October 27 by two major brands in China after a video circulated online in which the French football star apparently joked about former leader Mao Zedong. (Photo by Pedro PARDO / AFP via Getty Images) (Pedro PARDO / AFP via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sure enough, the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, of course, immediately criticized Mbappé's remarks.

"If you're going to get in bed with Communist China, if you're going to get in bed with somebody that isn't as open and free thinking as we are and Europeans are, then you better shut your damn mouth. You know, you better just sit back, take your money, and quit screwing around."

The freedoms that many athletes take for granted here are not present everywhere. And Dakich brought up that there's no awareness of how lucky they are to play where they do.

"You can be political here in the United States because we enjoy freedoms that others don't," he said. "But when you come at China, they react. This is going to cost Mbappé a ton of money. A ton. I mean, this is going to be something that he cannot recover from now. Does he care? Don't know. Should he care, don't know? I don't even a little bit.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"But I got to tell you, they always back down. Hell, you think LeBron James would practice his golf swing if he was in China listening to the Chinese anthem? Hell no. No, they're always back because it's big money."

That's the reality, that Mbappé and James and all the rest of them will do anything to avoid taking a hit to their wallet, no matter how embarrassing and humiliating it is. They're the first to speak out on social issues when it's free, and the first to back down when it matters.

title: Valkyries stars tells fans to ‘call in sick’ for Game 6 as early WNBA Finals tipoff sparks fan reaction
excerpt:

Game 6 of the WNBA Fina...
body_text:
"The Atlanta Dream have run into another arena scheduling conflict and may be forced to play Game 6 in the Gateway Center. The Gateway Center hosts about as many as my house."

Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries has been moved up to 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday to give State Farm Arena enough time to get the building ready for an NBA game that evening.

The early tipoff could create a challenge for fans in California, where the game will begin at 9:30 a.m. PT. The Valkyries defeated the Dream in Monday’s Game 5 in San Francisco to take a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven series, meaning Game 6 could determine the WNBA champion.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

While championship series games, especially potential championship-clinching contests, are routinely played in prime time, Thursday’s less-than-ideal scheduling doesn’t appear likely to stop Valkyries fans from tuning in to watch their favorite team.

Chase Center is seen before Game 5 of the WNBA finals between the Golden State Valkyries and the Atlanta Dream on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in San Francisco, California. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

WNBA FINALS GAME 6, A POTENTIAL TITLE-CLINCHER, WILL BE HELD IN THE AFTERNOON ON THURSDAY

Warriors coach Steve Kerr is among those who plan to tune in, even if he’s having breakfast when the game is starting. "We’ll have a day off that day, so, yeah, I’ll be watching," he said.

Several of the WNBA Finals games have drawn record ratings, showing how much interest there is in the league, this series and its athletes. The Valkyries have sold out every game since they began as an expansion franchise last year.

Shaunice Christmas-Miller and her wife, Kendall, have attended every home playoff game this season at Chase Center. Their jobs allow them to be flexible and work from home Thursday. Nevertheless, the couple believes the fan base will still show up Thursday.

"Absolutely, they will definitely find a way," Shaunice said.

State Farm Arena will host WNBA Finals Game 6 on Thursday afternoon before the Atlanta Hawks face the Cleveland Cavaliers that night. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Valkyries co-owner Peter Guber was largely unconcerned that the franchise’s devoted home crowd would come together when it matters most, despite morning challenges such as commuter traffic heading into San Francisco for a watch party.

DREAM COACH KARL SMESKO CALLS WNBA FINALS OFFICIATING ‘JUST RIDICULOUS’ AS ANGEL REESE ALSO QUESTIONS REFS

Supporters have been invited to gather outside Chase Center’s Thrive City viewing area beneath the big screen.

Shaunice added that she wishes everybody involved had considered the various options well in advance to avoid such last-minute scrambling.

Golden State Valkyries fans cheer before Game 5 of the WNBA Finals against the Atlanta Dream at Chase Center in San Francisco, California, on Oct. 26, 2026. (Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

"They should have thought ahead for the whole seven-game series," Shaunice noted. "The women deserve primetime slots."

Others expressed their feelings on social media.

Rapper Flavor Flav posted Tuesday: "Thursday is a paid holiday. Because Flavor Flav said so." Included in his post was a photo of a note directed to bosses everywhere as a permission slip of sorts requesting excused absences for employees, signed by Flavor Flav with dual titles beneath his name — "The World’s Greatest Hype Man" and "Official Supporter of Women’s Sports."

Ole Miss women’s coach Yolett McPhee-McCuin sounded off.

"I’d rather play anywhere else than have a 12:30 tip for a WNBA FINALS game man! Not a good look! For fans and for the players," she posted on X. "Just my 2cents that no one asked for."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Golden State coach Natalie Nakase and her players have focused all along on what they can control, and this certainly isn’t one of those things.

But there were some clever postgame offerings:

"Call in sick, I recommend it," point guard Veronica Burton cracked.

"Yeah, right? Y’all know how to fake a cough, didn’t we all do that?" teammate Kiah Stokes added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Golden State guard Kaila Charles has no doubt the Valkyries will adjust for the early tipoff.

"I think it’s a good thing that we’re able to play in a bigger arena so that they can have more people come and support women’s basketball," Charles said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rules
excerpt:
Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions

Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding ...
body_text:
Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions

Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210 million barrels of oil – equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices stemming from the US war in Iran.

In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, praised what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.

According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic ft of natural gas.

Although some oil and gas executives spoke publicly in favor of the landmark methane rule, industry trade groups and corporations worked behind the scenes to gut the methane regulations, according to trade association materials and records obtained via the Freedom of Information Act by Fieldnotes, an oil and gas watchdog organization.

The 2024 methane rule required oil and gas operators to eliminate and minimize leaking, flaring and venting of methane and of volatile organic compounds, which are harmful to human health.

It was the first time the federal government had set nationwide requirements to limit methane emissions from existing oil and gas facilities. An earlier rule finalized under the Obama administration in 2016 applied to new and modified sources. Under the rule’s super emitter program, companies had to investigate major leaks near oil and gas facilities detected by third parties using EPA-approved remote sensing technology.

In March 2025, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin announced that the agency was reconsidering the Biden-Harris regulations “to ensure that they do not prevent America from unleashing energy dominance and continuing our trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions”.

Last year, the US emitted more methane from its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world. Methane is responsible for at least a quarter of today’s warming.

Julia Kane, a researcher for Fieldnotes, said the Trump Environmental Protection Agency was giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they want. “The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” she said.

Records obtained by Fieldnotes, including calendar events, presentation slides and meeting request forms, show that industry groups and companies met with the EPA to discuss methane regulations at least 38 times during the current administration’s first year.

“I do think it’s just an extraordinary level of access,” Kane said, adding that industry groups themselves were pleasantly surprised by their access under Trump. For example, during a conference call with industry representatives last year, Independent Petroleum Association of America executive Lee Fuller described a discussion with EPA staff, saying: “It was one of the more fascinating meetings that we’ve ever had, just because they were suddenly willing to talk to us. And they were also suddenly willing to talk about things that we’ve been trying to get them to do for years, and they’ve never even let it come on to the radar screen.”

At a Trump rally in Corpus Christi earlier today, Trump shouted out Harold Hamm, saying the founder of Continental Resources was in the audience. In April, Continental Resources wrote a letter to the EPA pushing back against measures in the methane rule that prohibit routine flaring of associated gas.

Since the EPA announced it would no longer enforce oil and gas regulations in March 2025, oil and gas operators have leaked, vented or flared $7bn worth of natural gas, according to calculations by the Environmental Defense Fund.

Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the Trump administration was seeking to curtail the federal government’s ability to do anything to address climate pollution across all of the largest sectors responsible for emissions.

“What this administration is doing is enabling the worst polluters in the industry to continue to make ever more money off the back of American consumers while they’re wasting energy,” she said.

title: Taylor Swift’s hitmaker scolds Ed Sheeran, ‘stand the f--- up’ after Macklemore fallout
excerpt:
Ed Sheeran took rapper Macklemore off his tour after Macklemore stirred controversy with his pro-Palestine remarks on stage. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

Grammy-winning producer Jack Antonoff said Ed Shee...
body_text:
Ed Sheeran took rapper Macklemore off his tour after Macklemore stirred controversy with his pro-Palestine remarks on stage. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

Grammy-winning producer Jack Antonoff said Ed Sheeran missed a "massive" opportunity to "stand the f--- up" to billionaire interests, criticizing the English singer for removing Macklemore from his tour over the rapper’s remarks on Israel-Palestinian conflict.

Antonoff, lead singer for the band Bleachers and producer behind some of Taylor Swift’s biggest hits, made the scathing rebuke in a recent interview with The Guardian, more than a month after Sheeran faced backlash over Macklemore’s removal from the Loop Tour following the rapper’s calls for "Free Palestine" during his opening act.

"If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy. They’re going to let some f---ing promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside," Antonoff told the outlet.

COLIN KAEPERNICK ACCUSES NFL OF 'COLLUDING' AGAINST MACKLEMORE AMID 'FREE PALESTINE' CONTROVERSY

Jack Antonoff and Taylor Swift attend the 65th Grammy Awards at Crypto.com Arena on Feb. 5, 2023, in Los Angeles, California. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was among a group of NFL team owners who reportedly threatened to bar Sheeran’s stadium performances if Macklemore was included in the lineup.

Antonoff argued that Sheeran should have canceled the tour and staged free concerts outside the venues rather than give in to pressure from billionaires.

"[Ed Sheeran] missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there: just cancel the whole f---ing tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a f---ing billionaire tell you what to do," Antonoff said. "The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the f--- up."

KATHY GRIFFIN SAYS ED SHEERAN SHOULD HAVE TOLD ROBERT KRAFT TO 'GO F--- YOURSELF' OVER MACKLEMORE

Sheeran addressed the controversy during his Philadelphia tour stop, saying in part: "What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on Oct. 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate."

Several other artists scheduled to open for Sheeran, including Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham, dropped out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, who has doubled down on his message with a "Free Palestine Tour."

Antonoff, who has also voiced support for a "free Palestine," praised Macklemore for speaking out. The Jewish artist said he has "felt way more emboldened to say it now."

"It’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say," said the producer.

ED SHEERAN APOLOGIZES FOR MACKLEMORE BACKLASH, ENCOURAGES UNITY AT FIRST CONCERT SINCE FALLOUT

Macklemore performs at St. Anne's Park on June 4, 2025, in Dublin, Ireland. (Redferns)

Film critic and Hollywood in Toto founder and editor Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that Antonoff does not care about free speech, arguing that his comments are an attempt to gain approval within his industry.

"Jack doesn't sound well-informed, either about Middle East politics or his own business," Toto said in a statement. "If Sheeran scrapped his tour, how many workers would lose their jobs? And, if he did an alternative tour, how would they get paid?"

"He knows it's acceptable within his industry to blanketly bash billionaires, a lazy, thoughtless attack and do a variation of ‘Free Palestine,'" Toto continued. "He's trying to curry favor within his industry. Sadly, it might just work."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Sheeran and Macklemore for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Criminal case against alleged Bondi terrorist delayed amid ‘unprecedented’ investigation
excerpt:
Naveed Akram, 24, has been charged with 78 offences after allegedly committing a terrorist act. The case has been adjourned until February

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates
...
body_text:
Naveed Akram, 24, has been charged with 78 offences after allegedly committing a terrorist act. The case has been adjourned until February

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The criminal case against Naveed Akram for his alleged role in the Bondi terror attack faces more delays after an “unprecedented” investigation by the joint counter-terrorism team.

The matter will not return to court until 24 February after it was adjourned on Wednesday before Sydney’s Downing Centre local court. Prosecutors expect to be ready to certify the charges against Akram, who is yet to enter a plea, by that date.

Akram, 24, and his father, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, allegedly murdered 15 people after opening fire at a Hanukah festival at Bondi beach on 14 December. Forty people were injured.

Naveed Akram, who survived a shootout with police, has been charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one count of committing a terrorist act that investigators allege may have been “inspired by Isis”. Sajid Akram was shot and killed by police at the scene.

Akram was charged with 59 offences in December, with 19 more added in April as the investigation progressed.

The prosecutor, Danielle New, made the application for the adjournment, without opposition from Akram’s defence team, on Wednesday. She said prosecutors had now completed their brief of evidence, which had also been beset by delays due to the sheer volume of evidence involved in the case.

The judge, Karen Stafford, granted the adjournment after New argued more time was needed so investigators could consult the Akrams’ alleged victims and next of kin on the charges laid against Akram ahead of the offences being certified before the court.

This certification process is a standard step in a criminal case, whereby prosecutors formally list the offences proceeding to trial.

New said her team did not want to “rush” the consultations and were conscious that Hanukah was approaching, as well as the Christmas holidays and summer shutdown period for the courts.

“It’s important the crown goes over everything again, to make sure no person’s narrative is left untold,” New told the court.

New said the brief of evidence included thousands of witness statements, medical records, financial statements and purchases made by the Akrams, and footage from Bondi beach on the evening of the attack.

“The [joint counter-terrorism team] has engaged in an investigation the size of which has been unprecedented,” New told the court. “The commitment by all involved is nothing short of highly professional.”

In December, the police “fact sheet” – which was released via the courts and outlined the then allegations against Naveed Akram – alleged there was evidence that the pair “meticulously planned this terrorist attack for many months”. This allegedly included the creation of an “ISIS inspired” video, firearm training and the making of explosives.

The pair, police said in the document, allegedly undertook a “reconnaissance” visit to Bondi two days before the attack, visiting the footbridge from which they are accused of deliberately firing at those gathered at the Jewish festival.
